53	\begin{abstract}
54	Mixture-of-expert adapters with learned routers are a natural way to adapt frozen time series foundation models (TSFMs)---yet they \textbf{catastrophically fail} on TSFMs with instance normalization: routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$ because the normalization strips the per-window statistics the router needs. We isolate this \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse} through seven converging causal controls---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---while all eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism: normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped statistics. The resulting signal-ratio predictor identifies which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$), including where it does \emph{not} help (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA achieves \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$), generalizes across six backbones (two negative controls confirm normalization-specificity), and produces a \textbf{Frozen Paradox} where frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. A dual-stream extension, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}, achieves \textbf{parity-or-better with DLinear on $107/123$ cells} ($65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses), with $15/16$ losses at $H{\geq}192$ and $100\%$ on Timer-XL and Moirai-MoE.
55	\end{abstract}
56	
57	\section{Introduction}
58	\label{sec:intro}
59	
60	Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm}---provide powerful pretrained representations for temporal tasks. Once a TSFM is pretrained, a practical question determines whether it is useful in production: \textit{how should the adapter that connects it to a downstream task be designed?}
61	
62	\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.} Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. But real time series are non-stationary---ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions---and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable expert.
63	
64	\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation enables deployment regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve: multi-tenant cloud serving with hot-swappable adapters, on-device deployment with over-the-air adapter updates, and cross-task reuse (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes the primary per-dataset adaptation path.
65	
66	\textbf{The collapse problem.} This natural mixture-of-experts approach \emph{catastrophically fails} on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The root cause is \textbf{normalization-induced co-adaptation}: the dominant expert receives larger gradients, which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, creating a feedback loop that collapses within ${\sim}50$ training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Even with a frozen backbone, hidden-state routing still underperforms because RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish different input regimes. This is normalization-specific: Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does \emph{not} collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
67	
68	\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
69	
70	Our contributions are threefold:
71	
72	\textbf{(1)~A general principle: normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) proves that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes three \textbf{testable predictions}: (a)~a quantitative predictor $R(\mathcal{D})$ identifies which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) and which do not (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (confirmed: Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~the principle transfers across modalities (confirmed: ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet$+$InstanceNorm2d does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}). Seven converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
73	
74	\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm normalization-specificity.
75	
76	\textbf{(3)~Closing the DLinear gap---and explaining when it cannot close.} Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} adds a raw-input prediction branch and achieves parity-or-better with DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones ($65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses; \S\ref{sec:main_results}). The $16$ remaining losses cluster at long horizons ($15/16$ at $H{\geq}192$), with the lone $H{=}96$ loss on the smallest dataset (ETTh1, $+2.2\%$). Timer-XL ($12/12$) and Moirai-MoE ($15/15$) achieve $\mathbf{100\%}$.
77	
78	\section{Related Work}
79	
80	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
81	
82	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
83	
84	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep eleven such mechanisms on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no optimization trick can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design.
85	
86	\textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics---both recognizing that instance normalization discards predictive information. We identify a previously unknown consequence: RevIN destroys the per-window statistics that MoE routers require for discriminative gating. RR-MoA operationalizes the ``statistic re-injection'' insight specifically for routing.
87	
88	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
89

191	\subsection{Problem Formulation and Expert Pool}
192	
193	For a mixture of adapters to be effective, the expert pool must contain structurally diverse heads so that the router has meaningful choices. An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
194	
195	\textbf{Standard protocol.} Chronological train/val/test splits per the LTSF benchmark~\citep{zhou2021informer}: ETT-hourly (8640/2880/2880), ETT-minutely (34560/11520/11520), Weather/Electricity (60/20/20\%). Final evaluation uses the held-out test set.
196	
197	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
198	\label{sec:rrmoa}
199	
200	As shown in the introduction, routing on normalized hidden states fails because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:

200	As shown in the introduction, routing on normalized hidden states fails because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
201	\begin{equation}
202	\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}} \underbrace{\widetilde{w}_j}_{\text{sparse weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H}_\text{FM})}_{\text{deep embedding branch}},\quad
203	\mathcal{T} = \mathrm{TopK}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}),\, k\right),\;\;
204	\widetilde{w} = \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})\right)
205	\label{eq:rrmoa}
206	\end{equation}
207	where $G_\psi$ is a small Conv1d\,+\,pooling\,+\,linear gate ($\sim$1.1K params) operating directly on the raw time series, and each $\text{Expert}_k$ is a canonical adapter head. Routing is restricted to the Top-$k$ experts with the highest gate logits, so only $k$ of $K$ experts execute per sample. With $K{=}5$, $k{=}2$ we obtain $40\%$ of the dense FLOPs while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain (\S\ref{sec:topk}). The raw input preserves the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips away, enabling per-sample routing that reflects the physical characteristics of each time series window.
208	
209	\begin{algorithm}[h]
210	\caption{RR-MoA: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters with Top-$k$ sparse routing}
211	\label{alg:rrmoa}
212	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
213	\REQUIRE Strictly frozen TSFM $f_{\theta_\text{frozen}}$, raw input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L}$, $K$ expert adapters, sparsity $k\leq K$
214	\STATE $\mathbf{H}\leftarrow f_{\theta_\text{frozen}}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Deep embeddings; \textbf{no gradients} through $\theta$}
215	\STATE $\mathbf{g}\leftarrow G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Raw-signal gate logits, $\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times K}$}
216	\STATE $\mathcal{T}\leftarrow \mathrm{TopK}(\mathbf{g},\,k)$ \hfill \COMMENT{Per-sample indices of the $k$ selected experts}
217	\STATE $\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}\leftarrow \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathbf{g})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Renormalized over selected experts only}
218	\STATE \textbf{for each}\ $j \in \mathcal{T}$\ \textbf{do}
219	\STATE \quad $\mathbf{o}_j\leftarrow \text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Only the $k$ selected experts execute}
220	\STATE \textbf{end for}
221	\STATE $\mathbf{Y}\leftarrow \sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{w}_j\cdot \mathbf{o}_j$
222	\RETURN $\mathbf{Y}$
223	\end{algorithmic}
224	\end{algorithm}

226	\section{Experiments}
227	
228	\subsection{Setup}
229	
230	We evaluate RR-MoA on standard long-term forecasting benchmarks using five backbones, seven baselines, and up to five random seeds per configuration.
231	
232	\textbf{Backbones.} Our primary backbone is MOMENT-small~\citep{goswami2024moment} ($d_\text{model}{=}512$, 8 T5-style encoder blocks, internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}). We additionally evaluate MOMENT-large ($d_\text{model}{=}1024$, 24 blocks), Moirai-1.1-R-small~\citep{woo2024moirai} ($d_\text{model}{=}384$, 6 blocks, no RevIN), and Chronos-T5-small~\citep{ansari2024chronos} ($d_\text{model}{=}512$, 6 T5 encoder blocks, no RevIN) as a \emph{negative control} without instance normalization (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Primary results use a \emph{strictly frozen} backbone ($\theta$ not updated); freeze-level ablations appear in \S\ref{sec:freeze_ablation}.
233	
234	\textbf{Datasets and tasks.} ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2~\citep{zhou2021informer}, Weather (21 channels), and Electricity (321 channels)---standard LTSF benchmarks~\citep{godahewa2021monash, wen2023tssurvey}. Chronological train/val/test splits follow the LTSF protocol. We evaluate both long-term forecasting ($H{=}96$) and masked imputation (20\% reconstruction). All MSE values are reported on channel-wise StandardScaler-normalized inputs, following the standard LTSF convention~\citep{zhou2021informer, nie2023patchtst}. As a calibration anchor, DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} on our pipeline achieves $0.416$ (ETTh1), $0.322$ (ETTm1), $0.208$ (Weather)---consistent with published numbers (Appendix~\ref{app:dlinear}).
235	
236	\textbf{Training.} Adam optimizer, lr$=10^{-3}$, MSE loss, batch size 128, 15 epochs. Final reported numbers are 15-epoch test MSE. Multi-seed experiments use seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45, 46\}$ ($n{=}5$) for the core table; ablations use seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$.
237	
238	\textbf{Baselines.} We compare against seven baselines spanning the adapter design space. On the frozen backbone: (i)~three hand-designed \textit{fixed adapters} (linear, attention, conv), (ii)~\textit{LoRA}~\citep{hu2022lora} (108-run sweep; Appendix~\ref{app:lora_sweep}), (iii)~a \textit{TRACE-style} multi-scale adapter~\citep{li2025trace}, (iv)~an \textit{independent ensemble} of 5 experts (no router---isolates routing from diversity), and (v)~\textit{AdaMix}~\citep{wang2022adamix} (hidden-state MoE routing). With unfreezing: (vi)~\textit{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs). As a calibration anchor: (vii)~\textit{DLinear}~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} (trained from scratch, not a direct competitor). Together, these baselines test whether RR-MoA's gains come from routing, diversity, parameter count, or the frozen constraint.
239	
240	\textbf{Reproducibility.} All code, raw JSON results, per-seed routing-weight logs, and a self-verification script (\texttt{verify.py}) that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data are included in the supplementary material and will be open-sourced upon acceptance.
241	
242	\subsection{RR-MoA: Routing Collapse and Its Resolution}
243	\label{sec:main_results}
244	\label{sec:architectures}
245	\label{sec:freeze_ablation}
246	
247	This section proceeds in four steps: we first show that RR-MoA consistently outperforms fixed adapters (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), then diagnose why standard MoE routing fails (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}), demonstrate that no standard rescue mechanism recovers performance (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), and finally compare against a comprehensive baseline suite (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

277	
278	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). The explanation is that unfreezing the backbone triggers the co-adaptation loop (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared representation, collapsing routing. A frozen backbone prevents this loop, so the five-expert mixture retains its diversity advantage. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. SR-MoA independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Extended fine-tuning (50 epochs, cosine schedule) closes the gap by only ${\sim}4\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}
279	
280	\begin{proposition}[Gradient Co-Adaptation Drives Entropy Collapse]
281	\label{prop:frozen}
282	Consider a $2$-expert MoE with backbone $\mathbf{h}{=}A\mathbf{x}$, router $p{=}\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{h})$, loss $\ell{=}p\,\ell_1{+}(1{-}p)\,\ell_2$. Under gradient descent on $(A,\mathbf{w})$: \textup{(i)} the dominant expert's loss decreases faster ($\dot{\ell}_k \propto {-}p_k\|\nabla_\mathbf{h}\ell_k\|^2$), creating self-reinforcing collapse toward $p{\in}\{0,1\}$; \textup{(ii)} freezing $A$ breaks this loop (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
283	\end{proposition}
284	
285	{\looseness=-1 \textit{Remark.} Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear $A\mathbf{x}$; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}b confirms it in the full 8-block Transformer within ${\sim}50$ steps. Independent ensembles are $37$--$46\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}): learned routing, not mere diversity, drives gains.}

317	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why does standard MoE routing fail?} To understand the source of RR-MoA's advantage, we examine AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}, which uses the standard recipe of routing on hidden states. Table~\ref{tab:adamix} shows that AdaMix collapses to a single expert whenever backbone layers are unfrozen: entropy reaches $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations and stays below $0.55$ in the remaining 5. The green rows reveal the cause: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy from $0.000$ to $0.66$--$1.32$, proving that normalization is the causal mechanism (BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm produce the same collapse; Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}). The causal contrast is sharpest when comparing backbones directly (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}): under identical last-4 unfreezing on identical data, MOMENT entropy crashes to $0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps while Timer-XL (which lacks RevIN) stays at $1.60$ for all $400$ steps---opposite trajectories from the same code.}

336	In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters---exactly as Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
337	
338	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep eleven standard MoE rescue mechanisms---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, no optimization-side trick can compensate.
339	
340	\textbf{Self-routing and architecture-agnostic validation.} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, we test two additional controls. First, Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA)~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree}: each expert contains its own sigmoid gate---no external router. On raw input, SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). The same architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. Second, replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}). Both confirm the diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. \textbf{Summary of converging controls:} (C1)~RevIN ablation recovers entropy (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, green rows); (C2)~opposite trajectories on MOMENT vs Timer-XL (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}); (C3)~BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm collapse identically (Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}); (C4)~11 rescue mechanisms fail (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}); (C5)~raw-input AdaMix router recovers (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}); (C6)~SR-MoA raw vs hidden ($+87$--$768\%$; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}); (C7)~cross-modality replication on ViT (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}).

371	\textbf{Closing the DLinear gap.} DLinear (49K params, trained from scratch) achieves lower absolute MSE than frozen-backbone adapters (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, grey rows). 391	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass and dose-response.} Replacing the router's raw input with RevIN-normalized input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$ while entropy stays high (Table~\ref{tab:router_input}, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}), confirming the router relies on the \emph{content} of the stripped statistics, not merely the bypass path. A dose-response interpolation $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$ reveals a \emph{phase transition} (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs): MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), while entropy stays in $[1.43, 1.57]$---normalization renders routing uninformative without reducing diversity. A temporal-shuffle ablation confirms routing depends on $(M,\Sigma)$ statistics, not temporal ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}

452	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experimental evidence above converges on a clear mechanism, but relies on empirical observations. We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into three components: mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$, discarding $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$. The following proposition quantifies how much routing information is lost.
453	
454	\begin{proposition}[Routing Information Loss Under Instance Normalization]
455	\label{thm:mi_decomp}
456	Let $X$ be a random input window, $E \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ the expert assignment produced by any deterministic router, and $S = (X - M)/\Sigma$ the RevIN-normalized shape.
457	\begin{enumerate}
458	    \item[\textup{(i)}] \textbf{Exact decomposition.} $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S) \geq 0$.
459	    \item[\textup{(ii)}] \textbf{Unconditional quantitative bound.} Without any independence assumption,
460	    \[
461	        I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;\geq\; I(M, \Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M, \Sigma;\, S),
462	    \]
463	    where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M, \Sigma;\, S) \geq 0$ measures the ``leakage'' of stripped statistics through the shape.  Equality (tightness) holds iff $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ given $E$.
464	    \item[\textup{(iii)}] \textbf{Full-information corner.} If the router depends \emph{entirely} on the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), then $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the \emph{entire} routing distribution in nats.
465	    \item[\textup{(iv)}] \textbf{Signal ratio as sufficient-statistic proxy.} Since Part~(iii) establishes that $(M,\Sigma)$ are sufficient statistics for $E$ when the router depends entirely on them, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ measures the variance contribution of these sufficient statistics relative to the residual shape---a monotone proxy for the \emph{potential} routing information in the stripped statistics. The leakage $\varepsilon$ varies by dataset ($0.09$--$1.26$ nats via CCA; cross-validated within ${\pm}0.2$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}); $R(\mathcal{D})$ is validated at $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ across nine datasets. \textbf{Tightness:} direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via held-out classifier confirms normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy; the bound~(ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}).\footnote{$H(E \mid S)$ does not correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$); $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts improvement because it measures routing \emph{potential}, not the MI loss itself.}
466	\end{enumerate}
467	\end{proposition}
468	
469	Full proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}; rate-distortion interpretation and phase-transition formalization in Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}. \textit{Remark.} KSG cross-check (${\pm}0.26$ nats) confirms leakage estimates hold beyond Gaussianity. \textbf{Independent validation:} training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as an \texttt{nn.Parameter}, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}).
470	
471	\textbf{Quantitative prediction.} The \emph{routing signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\text{Var}(S)}$ serves as a monotone proxy for the MI bound. Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} validates this across nine LTSF benchmarks: $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI: $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$). Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier: the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.

545	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone} RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). On Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins \textbf{18/18} by $3$--$31\%$. On Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, which already contains sparse internal experts, RR-MoA still improves \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $37$--$90\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe})---confirming that adapter-level routing and backbone-internal routing are complementary. Two \textbf{negative controls} validate the diagnosis: Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, which lack instance normalization, show no routing collapse (entropy $1.48$--$1.61$) and RR-MoA provides no advantage (\textbf{4/18} wins, within chance)---exactly as Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}).}
546	
547	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Sparse routing, multi-horizon, and task generalization.}\label{sec:topk}
548	Top-2 sparse routing adds only $4.3$\,ms latency ($+10\%$) while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain. Scaling the expert pool from $K{=}3$ to $K{=}20$ changes MSE by less than $5\%$; notably, AdaMix at $K{=}15$ or $20$ maintains high entropy ($2.4$--$2.7$) yet its MSE remains $2$--$6{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA, confirming that the routing failure is informational rather than capacity-limited. RR-MoA's advantage extends beyond the primary horizon: it wins \textbf{24/24} configurations across $H{\in}\{96, 192, 336, 720\}$ and generalizes to imputation ($7/8$ datasets, $-44\%$ to $-77\%$) and classification ($86.5\%$ on BasicMotions; Appendix~\ref{app:topk},~\ref{app:imputation}).}
549	
550	\section{Conclusion}
551	
552	We identified \emph{normalization-induced co-adaptation} as the root cause of MoE routing collapse on time series foundation models. Seven causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). \textbf{RR-MoA} breaks the collapse by routing on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. A dual-stream extension, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}, matches or beats DLinear on \textbf{108/123 cells} across six backbones---with $15/16$ losses at $H{\geq}192$ and $\mathbf{100\%}$ on Timer-XL and Moirai-MoE.
553	
554	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on \emph{any} normalized backbone (time series, vision, or other modalities), compute the routing signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$. Values above $0.5$ predict that raw routing will help substantially; values below $0.2$ predict it will not (validated cross-modally; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}).
555	
556	\textbf{Limitations.} A small gap remains on ETTh1 ($+2.2\%$ vs DLinear). Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested. Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers only linear backbones, though Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers. $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses only first moments; higher-order statistics may improve prediction on outlier datasets such as Solar.

935	\section{Proposition Proofs}
936	\label{app:proofs}
937	
938	\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}} (Routing Information Loss Under RevIN, revised form).
939	
940	\begin{proof}
941	Throughout, $X$ denotes a raw window, $(M,\Sigma)$ its per-window mean/scale, $S = (X-M)/\Sigma$ its RevIN-normalized shape, and $E$ a deterministic (possibly randomized) router assignment. The map $(X) \mapsto (S, M, \Sigma)$ is invertible, so $I(X; Y) = I(S, M, \Sigma; Y)$ for any $Y$, and in particular $I(X; E) = I(S, M, \Sigma; E)$.
942	
943	\emph{Part (i): Exact decomposition.} By the chain rule of mutual information applied to $(S, M, \Sigma; E)$,
944	\begin{align*}
945	I(X; E) \;=\; I(S, M, \Sigma;\, E) \;=\; I(S;\, E) + I(M, \Sigma;\, E \mid S).
946	\end{align*}
947	Rearranging, $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma;\, E \mid S) \geq 0$. This identity holds \emph{without any independence assumption} between $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$.
948	
949	\emph{Part (ii): Unconditional quantitative bound.} We bound the conditional mutual information $I(M,\Sigma; E \mid S)$ from below in terms of the \emph{unconditional} quantities $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ and $I(M,\Sigma; S)$. Applying the chain rule two different ways to $I(M,\Sigma; E, S)$,
950	\begin{align*}
951	I(M,\Sigma;\, E, S) &= I(M,\Sigma;\, S) + I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \qquad\text{(expand $S$ first)} \\
952	                    &= I(M,\Sigma;\, E) + I(M,\Sigma;\, S \mid E) \qquad\text{(expand $E$ first).}
953	\end{align*}
954	Equating and solving for $I(M,\Sigma; E \mid S)$,
955	\[
956	I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \;=\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S) \;+\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S \mid E).
957	\]
958	Since $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E) \geq 0$ (mutual information is non-negative), we obtain
959	\[
960	I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;=\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \;\geq\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S),
961	\]
962	where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M,\Sigma; S) \geq 0$ is the \emph{leakage} of location-scale statistics into the shape. Equality (tightness) holds iff $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E) = 0$, i.e.\ iff $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$ are conditionally independent given $E$. In particular, unconditional independence $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ implies $\varepsilon = 0$ and recovers the classical $I(X;E) - I(S;E) \geq I(M,\Sigma; E)$ bound as a corollary.
963	
964	\emph{Part (iii): Full-information corner.} Suppose the router depends entirely on the stripped statistics: $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M, \Sigma)$, which means $p(E \mid S, M, \Sigma) = p(E \mid M, \Sigma)$. Then the Markov chain $S \to (M,\Sigma) \to E$ holds, and by the DPI $I(S; E) \leq I(M,\Sigma; E)$ but also $I(S; E) = 0$ whenever the Markov chain's first step $S \to (M,\Sigma)$ conveys no information (which holds when $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$). In the full-information corner case $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ and $E$ determined by $(M,\Sigma)$, we have $I(S;E) = 0$ and $I(X;E) = I(M,\Sigma;E) = H(E) - H(E \mid M,\Sigma) = H(E)$. Hence $I(X;E) - I(S;E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution.
965	
966	\emph{Part (iv): Empirical leakage and signal ratio.} We measure the leakage $\varepsilon = I(M,\Sigma; S)$ via two independent methods.
967	
968	\emph{Gaussian reference.} Since $(M,\Sigma)$ is 2-dimensional, there are at most 2 canonical correlations $\rho_1, \rho_2$ between $(M,\Sigma)$ and the shape $S$. For jointly Gaussian variables, $I(M,\Sigma; S) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^2 \log(1 - \rho_i^2)$. This yields $\varepsilon_\text{Gauss}$ ranging from $0.09$ nats (Weather, $\rho_\text{max}{=}0.35$) to $1.26$ nats (Exchange, $\rho_\text{max}{=}0.89$). The leakage is \emph{not} uniformly small --- datasets with strong trend-seasonality coupling (Exchange, ETTh2) have substantial shape-level encoding of location-scale statistics.
969	
970	\emph{Distribution-free cross-check.} Because canonical correlations capture only linear dependence, we cross-validate with the KSG $k$-nearest-neighbor MI estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}, which requires no distributional assumptions. We project $S$ onto its 2 canonical variates with respect to $(M,\Sigma)$ and estimate the $2$-vs-$2$ MI with $k{=}5$ neighbors on $N{\geq}888$ samples per dataset. The KSG estimates agree with the Gaussian reference within $\pm 0.26$ nats across all 9 datasets, confirming that nonlinear dependence does not substantially inflate the leakage beyond the CCA-captured linear component.
971	
972	\emph{Tightness condition.} The bound~(ii) is informative when $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$. Since $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ increases with the location-scale variance, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ is a monotone proxy for the tightness of the bound. This explains the $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ correlation: high-$R$ datasets (Exchange, $R{=}2.17$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$, producing large gains ($-68.5\%$); low-$R$ datasets (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \approx \varepsilon$, producing no gain ($+2.9\%$).
973	\end{proof}
974	
975	\textbf{Remark on the classical form.} The earlier version assumed $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ outright. The revised form~(ii) keeps $\varepsilon$ explicit and Part~(iv) measures it via both parametric (CCA) and non-parametric (KSG) methods, eliminating the independence assumption. Part~(v) bypasses the bound entirely by directly measuring $H(E \mid S)$, confirming the gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats (Table~\ref{tab:mi_tightness}). The agreement between Gaussian reference and distribution-free KSG estimates ($\pm 0.26$ nats) confirms the CCA-based values are reliable despite non-Gaussianity.
976	
977	\subsection{Theoretical Depth of Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}}
978	\label{app:prop2_depth}
979	
980	While the MI decomposition in Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} is algebraically a chain-rule identity, it has deeper information-theoretic content when connected to rate-distortion theory and phase transitions.
981	
982	\textbf{Rate-distortion interpretation of $R(\mathcal{D})$.}
983	Instance normalization is a \emph{deterministic lossy compression}: it maps $X \mapsto S$, discarding $(M, \Sigma)$. In rate-distortion theory~\citep{cover2006elements}, this compression has rate $R_\text{strip} = I(X; M, \Sigma \mid S)$ and distortion (for routing) $D_\text{route} = H(E \mid S) - H(E \mid X) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S)$, which is exactly Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i). Under Gaussianity, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ is proportional to the rate-distortion slope at the normalization operating point: it measures how much routing capacity is consumed by the statistics that normalization strips. Specifically, if the joint $(M, \Sigma, S)$ is multivariate Gaussian, then $I(M, \Sigma; E) \propto \log(1 + R(\mathcal{D}))$ (by the Gaussian mutual information formula), making $R(\mathcal{D})$ a \emph{monotone surrogate for the bits lost to normalization}. The validated $\rho = -0.88$ correlation (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}) is thus not a statistical coincidence but a consequence of this rate-distortion structure.
984	
985	\textbf{Phase-transition formalization.}
986	The dose-response experiment (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}) interpolates the router input as $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$. Under the Gaussian model, the effective routing signal power is:
987	\[
988	    P_\text{route}(\alpha) \;=\; (1{-}\alpha)^2 \cdot [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] \;+\; \alpha^2 \cdot \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)} \;+\; 2\alpha(1{-}\alpha)\,\mathrm{Cov}_\text{cross}
989	\]
990	where the cross-covariance term $\mathrm{Cov}_\text{cross}$ is small because $M, \Sigma$ are approximately orthogonal to $S$ (Part~ii leakage $\varepsilon$ bounds this). The routing discriminability crosses the router's noise floor at a critical threshold $\alpha^*$. For datasets where $(M, \Sigma)$ dominate routing (Part~iii regime), this threshold satisfies:
991	\[
992	    \alpha^* \;\approx\; \frac{R(\mathcal{D})}{R(\mathcal{D}) + 1}
993	\]
994	For the median $R(\mathcal{D}) = 0.67$ across the benchmark, this predicts $\alpha^* \approx 0.40$, consistent with the empirical observation that MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha \leq 0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha = 1.0$ ($+283\%$; Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). The sharpness of the transition arises from the softmax router's exponential sensitivity: when the input signal-to-noise ratio $P_\text{route}(\alpha) / P_\text{noise}$ drops below ${\sim}1$, routing weights converge to uniform regardless of the underlying expert relevance.
995	
996	\textbf{Information bottleneck connection.}
997	The RevIN-encoder pipeline implements a form of the information bottleneck~\citep{tishby2000ib}: it compresses $X$ into a representation $H = f_\theta(S)$ that is optimized for downstream prediction while discarding ``irrelevant'' variability (the per-window location-scale statistics). The routing MI loss from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) is the price paid for this compression \emph{at the routing decision point}. This connects to a broader principle: any architecture that bottlenecks information for one objective (prediction) can inadvertently destroy information needed for another (routing). The vision cross-modality control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) confirms this is not RevIN-specific: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patches creates the same bottleneck, while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does not---because spatial features are not the routing signal for classification.
998	
999	\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:hierarchy}} (Strict Head-Level Hierarchy: $\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$).
1000	
1001	\begin{proof}
1002	\emph{$\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subseteq \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$}: Each $c \in \mathcal{C}_\text{head}$ is, by Definition~\ref{def:discrete_head}, a pooling strategy followed by an MLP head. Both components are expressible as template derivations of the form $S \to \text{Pool}\cdot\text{MLP}\cdot\text{Output}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:grammar}), so $c$ lies in $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$. \emph{Strict}: $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ additionally admits Conv1d pooling and SiLU activations absent from $\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$.
1003	
1004	\emph{$\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subseteq \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$}: Every template derivation produces a valid Python program satisfying Definition~\ref{def:code}. \emph{Strict}: $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ contains depthwise convolutions, batch normalization, residual connections, and learned positional weights---none derivable from the template grammar (Table~\ref{tab:expressiveness}).
1005	
1006	\emph{Orthogonality of LoRA and bottleneck configurations.} Configurations in $\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$ modify the backbone's attention projections (LoRA) or inject residual modules between encoder blocks (bottleneck). They are not head-level adapters and are therefore not members of $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ nor of $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ as defined (the code space is restricted to adapter classes operating on extracted hidden states, per Definition~\ref{def:code}). We compare against the LoRA variant separately under the strictly frozen backbone protocol in Table~\ref{tab:baselines}.
1007	\end{proof}
1008	
1009	\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}} (Gradient Co-Adaptation Drives Entropy Collapse).
1010	
1011	\begin{proof}
1012	Consider a single input $\mathbf{x}$ with backbone $\mathbf{h} = A\mathbf{x}$, router $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{h})$, and loss $\ell = p\,\ell_1(\mathbf{h}) + (1-p)\,\ell_2(\mathbf{h})$.
1013	
1014	\emph{Part (i): Unfrozen backbone.} The gradient with respect to $A$ is:
1015	\begin{equation*}
1016	\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial A} = p\,\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\mathbf{x}^\top + (1{-}p)\,\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\mathbf{x}^\top + (\ell_1 - \ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\,\mathbf{w}\mathbf{x}^\top
1017	\end{equation*}
1018	Under gradient descent $\dot{A} = -\eta\,\partial\ell/\partial A$, the induced change in expert~1's loss is:
1019	\begin{multline*}
1020	\dot{\ell}_1\big|_A = -\eta\|\mathbf{x}\|^2\!\Bigg[p\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2 + (1{-}p)\left(\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right)^{\!\top}\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}} \\
1021	 + (\ell_1{-}\ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\left(\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right)^{\!\top}\mathbf{w}\Bigg]
1022	\end{multline*}
1023	The first term (self-gradient) always decreases $\ell_1$. The second (cross-gradient) is negligible when expert gradients are approximately orthogonal---a condition that holds empirically once experts specialize to distinct input clusters (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_weights}). The third (loss-coupling) term is small early in training when $|\ell_1 - \ell_2| \ll \|\partial\ell_1/\partial\mathbf{h}\|$. Retaining only the dominant first term:
1024	\begin{equation*}
1025	\dot{\ell}_1\big|_A \approx -\eta\,p\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2
1026	\end{equation*}
1027	and analogously $\dot{\ell}_2\big|_A \approx -\eta\,(1{-}p)\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2$. When $p > 1{-}p$ (expert~1 dominates), $\ell_1$ decreases faster than $\ell_2$. The third term in $\partial\ell/\partial A$ further reinforces this: when $\ell_1 < \ell_2$, the factor $(\ell_1 - \ell_2) < 0$ drives $\dot{p} > 0$, pushing $p$ toward~1. Together these create the self-reinforcing loop: dominant expert gets more gradient $\to$ its loss drops faster $\to$ router increases its weight $\to$ it becomes more dominant.
1028	
1029	\emph{Part (ii): Frozen backbone.} When $A$ is fixed, $\dot{A} = 0$. The only dynamics are through $\mathbf{w}$:
1030	\begin{equation*}
1031	\dot{\mathbf{w}} = -\eta\,\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{w}} = -\eta\,(\ell_1 - \ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\,\mathbf{h}
1032	\end{equation*}
1033	This update adjusts routing weights based on current expert performance, but does \emph{not} reshape $\mathbf{h}$ to favor one expert. Without the $A$-mediated feedback loop, there is no systematic bias toward entropy collapse---the router converges to a stable allocation reflecting the static geometry of the fixed representation space.
1034	\end{proof}
1035	
1036	\textbf{Budget Sufficiency (Empirical).} All 14 tested search budgets $B\in[20,480]$ beat the conv baseline on both ETTh1 and ETTm1; MSE saturates around $B\!\approx\!60$ (Appendix~\ref{app:budget}). Evolutionary selection did not outperform random sampling in $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$.
1037	
1038	\section{AAS Search Details}
1039	\label{app:aas_details}
1040	
1041	The AAS loop maintains a population of 20 adapters over 12 generations (${\sim}240$ evaluations, 3-epoch fitness probes). Elitism preserves the top 2; an LLM variant generates candidates in the code space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$. Template-based generation achieves 100\% validity (vs.\ ${\sim}75\%$ for LLM).
1042	
1043	\subsubsection*{Template Grammar Production Rules}
1044	\label{app:grammar}
1045	
1046	\begin{align*}
1047	S &\rightarrow \nonterminal{Pool} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{MLP} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{Output} \\
1048	\nonterminal{Pool} &\rightarrow \text{MeanPool} \mid \text{MaxPool} \mid \text{LastToken} \mid \text{AttnPool} \mid \text{Conv1dPool} \\
1049	\nonterminal{MLP} &\rightarrow \nonterminal{Layer} \mid \nonterminal{Layer} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{MLP} \quad (\text{depth} \leq 3) \\
1050	\nonterminal{Layer} &\rightarrow \text{Linear}(d_\text{in}, d_\text{out}) \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{Act} \;\cdot\; \text{Dropout}(p) \\
1051	\nonterminal{Act} &\rightarrow \text{GELU} \mid \text{ReLU} \mid \text{SiLU} \mid \text{Tanh} \\
1052	\nonterminal{Output} &\rightarrow \text{Linear}(d_\text{last}, H)
1053	\end{align*}
1054	with $d_\text{out} \in \{64, 128, 192, 256, 384\}$ and $p \in \{0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$, yielding $|\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}| \approx 1{,}200$.
1055

1117	\section{Formal Definitions}
1118	\label{app:formal_defs}
1119	
1120	\begin{definition}[Adapter]
1121	Given a pretrained TSFM backbone $f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{B \times L} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d}$ that maps input time series to encoder hidden states, an \textbf{adapter} is a parameterized module $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ that maps hidden states to forecasts, where $\phi \in \Phi_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n_g}$ are trainable weights with $n_g \leq N_\text{max}$ (we set $N_\text{max} = 500{,}000$).
1122	\end{definition}
1123	
1124	\begin{definition}[Architecture Space]
1125	An \textbf{architecture space} $\mathcal{G}$ is a set of adapter specifications, where each $g \in \mathcal{G}$ determines: (i) a parameter space $\Phi_g$ and its dimensionality $n_g$, (ii) a computational graph defining the forward function $g_\phi(\cdot)$, and (iii) an initialization procedure for $\phi$.
1126	\end{definition}
1127	
1128	\begin{definition}[Discrete Configuration Space $\mathcal{C}$]
1129	The \textbf{discrete space} $\mathcal{C}$ is the Cartesian product of standard adapter hyperparameters:
1130	\begin{equation}
1131	\mathcal{C} = \underbrace{\{\text{lin, lora, bn}\}}_{\text{type}} \times \underbrace{\{8,16,32,64\}}_{\text{rank}} \times \underbrace{\{\text{mean, last, max, cls}\}}_{\text{pool}} \times \underbrace{\{\text{lin, mlp1, mlp2}\}}_{\text{head}} \times \cdots
1132	\end{equation}
1133	The full Cartesian product yields ${\sim}2{,}160$ configurations, of which ${\sim}144$ define distinct adapter \textit{computational graphs} when restricted to the head-only subspace.
1134	\end{definition}
1135	
1136	\begin{definition}[Head-Only Subspace $\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$]
1137	\label{def:discrete_head}
1138	The \textbf{head-only subspace} $\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{C}$ is the restriction of $\mathcal{C}$ to linear-probe configurations (pooling $\to$ MLP head), with LoRA rank $=0$ and no bottleneck.
1139	\end{definition}
1140	
1141	\begin{definition}[Code-Level Space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$]
1142	\label{def:code}
1143	The \textbf{code space} $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ is the set of all Python programs $p$ such that: (i)~$p$ defines a class \texttt{Adapter(nn.Module)} with \texttt{\_\_init\_\_(self, d\_model, output\_dim)} and \texttt{forward(self, h)} mapping $\mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$; (ii)~$n_p \leq N_\text{max}$; (iii)~$p$ uses only \texttt{\{torch, nn, F, math\}}.
1144	\end{definition}
1145	
1146	\begin{definition}[Template Space $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$]
1147	\label{def:template}
1148	The \textbf{template space} $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ is generated by a context-free grammar over 5 pooling types, 4 activations, variable MLP depths and widths, yielding $|\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}| \approx 1{,}200$ architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:grammar}).
1149	\end{definition}
1150	
1151	\begin{proposition}[Strict Head-Level Hierarchy]
1152	\label{prop:hierarchy}
1153	$\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$, and both inclusions are strict (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
1154	\end{proposition}
1155

1302	
1303	\textbf{What the router learns.} Per-sample routing decisions correlate with amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$), while Expert~2 (max-pool) handles low-amplitude windows and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude windows. The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the distribution tails, empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$ of Part~(iii) of Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.
1304	
1305	\begin{figure}[h]
1306	\centering
1307	\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/routing_viz.pdf}
1308	\caption{\textbf{Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(iii).}
1309	\label{fig:routing_viz}
1310	\end{figure}
1311	
1312	\textbf{Regime-specific adaptation.} Partitioning test windows into quartiles by amplitude, RR-MoA wins \textbf{all four quartiles} across all 9 (dataset, seed) pairs, with the largest improvement on quiet, low-amplitude windows (Q1: $4.6{\times}$ better, $0.24$ vs $1.09$ on ETTh1) and the smallest on volatile, high-amplitude windows (Q4: $1.3{\times}$, $1.54$ vs $1.97$).
1313	
1314	\textbf{Sufficient statistic router (SSR).} A router using only $[\mu(X_\text{raw}), \sigma(X_\text{raw})]$---functionally equivalent to a DishTS-style~\citep{fan2023dishts} routing mechanism that conditions on the exact statistics distribution-shift methods re-inject---degrades MSE by $+48\%$ on average ($+11\%$ to $+94\%$) vs.\ the Conv1d router across all 8 forecasting datasets. The degradation is largest on ETTm2 ($+94\%$) and Exchange ($+82\%$), and smallest on Weather ($+11\%$). While Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of the information loss, effective routing requires temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale statistics.
1315	
1316	\textbf{Temporal-shuffle ablation.} We route on a fixed temporal permutation of $X_\text{raw}$---destroying time ordering while preserving distributional statistics ($M$, $\Sigma$, histogram shape). Across 6 datasets (frozen, 5 seeds), shuffled routing performs within ${\pm}3\%$ of raw routing on 4/6 datasets (ETTh1 $+3.2\%$, ETTh2 $+1.2\%$, ETTm1 $-1.2\%$, Electricity $+0.7\%$), with Weather improving $-8.5\%$ and ETTm2 improving $-16.0\%$. Entropy remains high ($1.43$--$1.58$). This confirms that the Conv1d router primarily extracts distributional rather than temporal features from $X_\text{raw}$. Combined with the SSR result ($+48\%$ degradation using only $[\mu, \sigma]$), the picture is: distributional statistics provide the \emph{essential} routing signal, but temporal shape (which the shuffle preserves as histogram features in the Conv1d) provides an additional ${\sim}10\%$ refinement.
1317	
1318	\textbf{Router-Detached Gradient Flow (RDGF).} A variant that unfreezes the backbone but replaces routing-weighted gradients with uniform-average gradients ($\nabla_H \mathcal{L}_\text{backbone} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_k \nabla_H \mathcal{L}_k$) degrades MSE by $+35\%$ to $+100\%$ across three datasets. This confirms the Frozen Paradox is structural.
1319	
1320	\textbf{Spectral-temporal router (FFT-Router).} We augment the Conv1d router with explicit frequency-domain features: a parallel branch applies rFFT to $X_\text{raw}$, extracts the top-32 spectral amplitudes, and concatenates them with the Conv1d temporal embedding before the routing head. On the two datasets with matched dense-frozen baselines, FFT-Router \emph{degrades} MSE by $+6\%$ (Weather) and $+22\%$ (ETTm1). The Conv1d router already captures frequency-relevant patterns implicitly; adding explicit spectral features overparameterizes the router without improving routing quality.
1321	
1322	\textbf{Statistic-aware information bottleneck (SAIB).} An auxiliary loss forces the router's penultimate representation to predict the window-level $[\mu, \sigma]$---directly operationalizing Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. With SAIB coefficients $\lambda \in \{0.1, 1.0\}$, MSE is unchanged on ETTm1 ($0.395$ vs $0.397$ baseline) and slightly degraded on Weather ($0.250$ vs $0.236$). Routing entropy increases to $1.55$ (near-maximum $\log 5 = 1.61$), indicating the auxiliary loss disperses routing weights without improving forecast accuracy. This confirms the Conv1d router already encodes $\mu, \sigma$ without explicit supervision.
1323	
1324	\textbf{Instance-adaptive gating (IA-Gating).} In the dual-stream variant (Appendix~\ref{app:gap_closing}), we replace the static per-expert blending scalar $\alpha$ with a per-window gate $\gamma(X_\text{raw}) = \sigma(W_g \cdot z)$ where $z$ is the router's latent representation. Across 6 datasets (frozen, 3 seeds), IA-Gating wins on 4/6 (ETTh2 $-8.0\%$, ETTm2 $-6.4\%$, ETTm1 $-1.9\%$, Electricity $-0.4\%$) and loses on 2/6 (Weather $+6.1\%$, ETTh1 $+0.3\%$). The learned gates cluster tightly around $\gamma \approx 0.48$ across all datasets and windows, indicating the backbone's contribution is roughly constant per-window---which explains why the simpler static $\alpha$ performs comparably overall.

1419	\subsection{AdaMix Implementation Details}
1420	\label{app:adamix_details}
1421	
1422	Our AdaMix baseline follows \citet{wang2022adamix} with $K{=}5$ expert adapter heads identical to RR-MoA's canonical pool (mean, last, max, attention, conv1d). The router is a single linear layer $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^K$ operating on the mean-pooled hidden state, with softmax gating. We use a load-balancing auxiliary loss with coefficient $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$, matching AdaMix's original formulation. No stochastic routing, capacity factors, or noise injection are applied---these standard MoE safeguards do not address the normalization-specific signal loss we identify: when RevIN strips the per-window statistics that would distinguish samples, the router receives near-identical inputs regardless of stabilization strategy. This is confirmed empirically: load-balancing loss does not prevent collapse under unfreezing (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, entropy $= 0.000$ with $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$), while disabling RevIN recovers entropy to $0.66$--$1.32$ without any routing regularization.
1423	
1424	\textbf{Architecture-agnostic validation (AdaMix-Raw).} To confirm the diagnosis generalizes beyond RR-MoA, we replace AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input Conv1d router (identical architecture to RR-MoA's) while keeping AdaMix's expert heads and training loop unchanged. Table~\ref{tab:adamix_raw} shows results across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds (36 runs).

1470	MOMENT's RevIN applies instance normalization ($\mu{=}0$, $\sigma{=}1$ per window) \emph{before} the encoder, stripping mean and scale from every input. The RevIN inverse is applied after the encoder to restore original units for the loss computation, but the routing decision is made on post-RevIN hidden states. Moirai, Chronos, and Timer-XL apply only standard LayerNorm within each transformer block, which normalizes across the feature dimension but preserves per-window temporal statistics.

1472	\section{Normalization Generalization}
1473	\label{app:norm_generalization}
1474	
1475	To test whether routing collapse is specific to RevIN or a general property of instance-level normalization, we replace MOMENT's RevIN with two alternative normalizers---BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm (1 group)---and run AdaMix with last-4 unfreezing on ETTh1.
1476	
1477	\begin{table}[h]
1478	\centering
1479	\caption{\textbf{Routing collapse generalizes across normalizer types.} All three instance-level normalizers (RevIN, BatchNorm1d, GroupNorm) cause entropy collapse under unfreezing; removing normalization prevents collapse. Per-step trajectories logged over 400 optimizer steps on ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing, seed 42.}
1480	\label{tab:norm_generalization}
1481	\small
1482	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
1483	\toprule
1484	Normalizer & Entropy (step 0) & Entropy (step 400) & Collapses? \\
1485	\midrule
1486	RevIN (default) & $0.507$ & $0.000$ & \textbf{Yes} \\
1487	BatchNorm1d & $0.619$ & $0.004$ & \textbf{Yes} \\
1488	GroupNorm & $0.507$ & $0.000$ & \textbf{Yes} \\
1489	\midrule
1490	None (identity) & $0.623$ & $0.817$ & No \\
1491	\bottomrule
1492	\end{tabular}
1493	\end{table}
1494	
1495	All three normalizers cause entropy collapse to ${\leq}0.004$, while removing normalization entirely keeps entropy stable at $0.817$. The mechanism is the same in each case: the normalizer strips per-window statistics before the encoder, the router receives homogenized hidden states, and gradient co-adaptation amplifies the initial routing bias into full collapse. This confirms that the normalization-routing tension is a \emph{general} property of instance-level normalization, not a RevIN-specific artifact. Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts that collapse occurs specifically when the stripped statistics carry routing signal; a cross-modality control on ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) validates this: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$), while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does \emph{not}---exactly as the theory predicts.

1508	\toprule
1509	Backbone & Cond & Configuration & Entropy & Collapses? & Acc \\
1510	\midrule
1511	\multirow{4}{*}{ResNet-18} & A & Unfrozen + InstanceNorm2d & $1.475 \pm 0.021$ & No & $0.919$ \\
1512	& B & Frozen + InstanceNorm2d   & $0.992 \pm 0.041$ & No & $0.577$ \\
1513	& C & Unfrozen + No norm        & $\mathbf{0.184 \pm 0.260}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.921$ \\
1514	& D & Unfrozen + BatchNorm2d    & $1.476 \pm 0.031$ & No & $0.919$ \\
1515	\midrule
1516	\multirow{2}{*}{ViT-B/16} & E & Frozen + InstanceNorm1d   & $\mathbf{0.000 \pm 0.000}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.953$ \\
1517	& F & Frozen + No norm          & $0.494 \pm 0.130$ & No & $0.958$ \\
1518	\bottomrule
1519	\end{tabular}
1520	\end{table}
1521	
1522	\textbf{ResNet-18: normalization prevents collapse.} Without normalization (C), the unfrozen backbone co-adapts with the dominant expert, collapsing entropy to $0.184\pm0.260$---confirming Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}. Adding InstanceNorm2d (A) or BatchNorm2d (D) \emph{prevents} collapse ($1.48\pm0.02$), the \emph{opposite} of time series. Why: InstanceNorm2d strips per-channel spatial mean/variance, which carry negligible routing information for image classification (analogous to Traffic, $R{=}0.14$).
1523	
1524	\textbf{ViT-B/16: normalization causes collapse.} Extending to a Vision Transformer, InstanceNorm1d on frozen ViT patch embeddings collapses routing to $0.000\pm0.000$ (E), while the same backbone without normalization maintains healthy routing at $0.494\pm0.130$ (F). InstanceNorm1d normalizes per-channel across the 197-token sequence, stripping per-patch mean/scale statistics---structurally identical to RevIN on time-series windows. The routing signal in ViT resides partly in patch-level statistics (which patches are bright, high-contrast, textured), so stripping them degrades the router.
1525	
1526	\textbf{Unifying principle.} The collapse mechanism (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}) is modality-general. Whether normalization \emph{triggers} or \emph{prevents} collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal (Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}): ResNet spatial features survive InstanceNorm2d (no collapse); ViT patch statistics do not survive InstanceNorm1d (collapse). The same principle explains all five TS backbones, the ViT result, and the ResNet control.

1654	\section{Exact MI Loss and Bound Tightness}
1655	\label{app:mi_tightness}
1656	
1657	Since the router is deterministic ($E = \arg\max$), $I(X;E) = H(E)$ and the exact MI loss from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) reduces to $H(E \mid S)$. We estimate this directly: train the RR-MoA router on raw windows, extract expert assignments $E$, then train an MLP classifier ($512 \to 256 \to 128 \to K$) to predict $E$ from the RevIN-normalized shape $S$. The held-out cross-entropy (temperature-calibrated) gives $H(E \mid S)$.
1658	
1659	\begin{table}[h]
1660	\centering
1661	\caption{\textbf{Exact MI loss measurement and bound tightness} (3 seeds). $H(E \mid S)$ is the exact routing information lost to normalization. Retention $= I(S;E)/H(E)$. LB = lower bound from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii). Gap $= I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ via within-expert CCA.}
1662	\label{tab:mi_tightness}
1663	\small
1664	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccr@{}}
1665	\toprule
1666	Dataset & $H(E)$ & $H(E \mid S)$ & Ret\% & LB & Gap & $\Delta\%$ \\
1667	\midrule
1668	ETTh1       & 0.73 & 0.61 & 16.3 & 0.02 & 0.06 & $-43.2$ \\
1669	ETTh2       & 0.76 & 0.57 & 26.3 & 0.00 & 0.10 & $-71.0$ \\
1670	ETTm1       & 0.75 & 0.57 & 24.2 & 0.18 & 0.03 & $-51.1$ \\
1671	ETTm2       & 0.82 & 0.53 & 35.1 & 0.18 & 0.07 & $-77.2$ \\
1672	Weather     & 1.37 & 0.98 & 29.1 & 0.61 & 0.08 & $-44.6$ \\
1673	Electricity & 0.68 & 0.46 & 32.4 & 0.13 & 0.02 & $-26.8$ \\
1674	Traffic     & 0.63 & 0.44 & 24.6 & 0.19 & 0.02 & $+2.9$ \\
1675	Exchange    & 0.63 & 0.44 & 22.1 & 0.00 & 0.10 & $-66.5$ \\
1676	Solar       & 0.97 & 0.57 & 40.9 & 0.08 & 0.20 & $-32.9$ \\
1677	\bottomrule
1678	\end{tabular}
1679	\end{table}
1680	
1681	\textbf{Key findings.} (1)~Normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy across all nine datasets, confirming that RevIN universally degrades routing signal. (2)~The bound gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$), so the lower bound is empirically tight. (3)~Crucially, $H(E \mid S)$ does \emph{not} correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$, $p{=}0.77$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$). This distinction is informative: $H(E \mid S)$ measures how much routing information the \emph{specific trained router} loses, while $R(\mathcal{D})$ measures the \emph{potential} routing information that location-scale statistics could carry. The gap between these explains why some datasets with low MI loss still benefit substantially from raw routing---the router adapts to use whatever signal remains, but the \emph{quality} of that signal (captured by $R$) determines downstream task performance.
1682	
1683	\textbf{Synthetic validation.} On Gaussian mixture data ($K{=}5$ clusters) with analytically known MI, we sweep the shape-statistics correlation $\rho_{MS} \in [0, 0.9]$. At $\rho_{MS}{=}0$, the bound is tight (gap $= 0.19$ nats, $12\%$ of $\log K$). As $\rho_{MS}$ increases, the bound becomes vacuous ($\varepsilon$ exceeds $I(M,\Sigma;E)$), but $H(E \mid S)$ remains informative throughout---validating our direct measurement approach.

1839	\section{Deployment-Regime Motivation}
1840	\label{app:deployment}
1841	
1842	The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
1843	
1844	\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Per-tenant DLinear requires collecting, storing, and periodically retraining on each tenant's historical data ($O(N)$ training pipelines for $N$ tenants), whereas the frozen backbone is loaded once and adapter weights (${\sim}50$--$500$K parameters, ${\sim}0.2$--$2$\,MB) are swapped from host RAM in microseconds. At $N{=}1{,}000$ tenants, the adapter approach eliminates $1{,}000$ independent training jobs and enables instant onboarding of new tenants via zero-shot transfer---capabilities absent from per-tenant supervised baselines.
1845	
1846	\textbf{(ii) On-device and edge deployment.} One backbone is shipped with the device image; per-site adapters are updated over low-bandwidth links. Collecting each site's training data centrally is often impossible for privacy or latency reasons.
1847	
1848	\textbf{(iii) Cross-task reuse.} The same frozen backbone drives forecasting, imputation, and classification via different expert pools. We demonstrate the first two tasks explicitly in the main text.
1849

1870	
1871	The RR-MoA routing overhead ($+4.3$\,ms) is dominated by the sparse expert selection loop; the router itself (Conv1d + linear, ${\sim}1.1$K params) adds $<0.1$\,ms. At deployment scale, adapter swapping between tenants requires loading $426$K parameters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB) from host RAM---orders of magnitude cheaper than reloading a $35$M parameter backbone. At $N{=}100$ tenants, adapter-swapping throughput is $141$ tenants/sec. The memory footprint of a shared-backbone deployment ($1\times$ TSFM at $140$\,MB plus $100\times$ RR-MoA adapters at $1.7$\,MB each $= 310$\,MB total) is $45\times$ smaller than naively replicating the full backbone per tenant ($100 \times 140$\,MB $= 14\,000$\,MB). \textbf{Honest caveat:} this $45\times$ figure is against the naive per-tenant-TSFM baseline, which no rational deployer would run; against per-tenant DLinear ($100 \times 49$K parameters $= 19.6$\,MB total) the shared-TSFM approach is roughly $15\times$ \emph{larger}, not smaller. The memory argument for TSFMs over DLinear is therefore not the core motivation --- that role is played by cross-task reuse, zero-shot onboarding, and the elimination of $O(N)$ per-tenant training pipelines (see \S\ref{sec:intro} and Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}).

1900	
1901	The best extended schedule (50ep cosine + layer-wise LR decay) improves over the 15-epoch baseline by only $4$--$5\%$, while frozen RR-MoA maintains a $33$--$41\%$ advantage. This confirms the Frozen Paradox is not an optimization artifact: unfreezing is fundamentally counterproductive when RevIN strips routing information.
1902	
1903	\textbf{Causal proof via RevIN ablation.} Disabling RevIN inside MOMENT dramatically recovers full-FT performance: ETTh1 ($1.063 \to 0.490$, $-54\%$), ETTm1 ($0.910 \to 0.364$, $-60\%$), Weather ($0.481 \to 0.187$, $-61\%$). With RevIN disabled, full-FT matches or exceeds supervised baselines---confirming that RevIN, not the optimization protocol, is the root cause of the paradox.
1904	
1905	\textbf{Adapter training budget.} Extending adapter-only training (frozen backbone) from 15 to 50 epochs improves RR-MoA by $8$--$14\%$: ETTh1 ($0.690 \to 0.633$), ETTm1 ($0.572 \to 0.494$), Weather ($0.289 \to 0.250$). This narrows the supervised gap modestly but does not close it, consistent with the representation-bottleneck diagnosis: additional adapter training cannot recover information the backbone's normalization discarded. The remaining gap reflects the information ceiling of frozen backbone representations, not insufficient optimization of the adapter.
1906	
1907	\section{Closing the DLinear Gap}
1908	\label{app:gap_closing}
1909	\label{app:gap_closing_ext}
1910	
1911	A good diagnosis should be \emph{actionable}: identifying the root cause of a performance gap should point directly to how to close it. Our diagnosis pinpoints the DLinear gap as information destruction by the normalization--encoding pipeline (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}): experts operate on hidden states from which RevIN and patching have stripped fine-grained temporal structure. This diagnosis makes a clear architectural prediction: \emph{if we restore raw-signal access to the experts, the gap should close.} We test this prediction with three architectures.
1912	
1913	We test three architectures that provide experts with raw-input access while preserving the frozen-backbone paradigm and RR-MoA routing:
1914	
1915	\textbf{(1)~Dual-Stream.} Each expert blends a backbone branch (existing adapter head on $\mathbf{H}$) with a raw branch (MLP on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$) via a learnable per-expert scalar $\alpha_k$: $\mathbf{y}_k = \sigma(\alpha_k)\cdot\text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H}) + (1{-}\sigma(\alpha_k))\cdot\text{MLP}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$.
1916	
1917	\textbf{(2)~Raw-Input Expert.} A 6th expert operating directly on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ (bypassing the backbone) is added to the pool; the router decides per-sample whether to use backbone-based or raw-input experts.
1918	
1919	\textbf{(3)~Multi-Resolution.} Each expert concatenates projected raw features with pooled hidden-state features before forecasting: $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{MLP}([\text{Proj}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \text{Pool}_k(\mathbf{H})])$.
1920

Dual-stream experts that access both hidden states and raw input narrow the gap from $+33$--$75\%$ to $+9$--$11\%$ and \textbf{beat DLinear on Weather}. Learned $\alpha{\approx}0.49$ confirms the backbone contributes complementary information when combined with raw access.}

1940	\textbf{Result.} Dual-stream experts reduce the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5\%$---an $11\times$ reduction---and \emph{beat} DLinear on Weather ($0.198$ vs $0.208$, $p{=}0.03$, paired $t$-test). The learned blend parameters $\alpha_k \approx 0.49$ across all five experts confirm that the backbone provides complementary information when experts can also access the raw signal: neither branch alone suffices.
1941	
1942	\textbf{Extension to ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity.} Running all four variants on the three remaining forecasting datasets yields consistent gap closure (Table~\ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}). Dual-stream wins on Electricity at $+8\%$ and matches well on ETTm2 ($+26\%$), while \textbf{multi-resolution wins on ETTh2 at $+7.7\%$}---the tightest new gap-closing result on any dataset we did not originally study. Multi-resolution also performs competitively on ETTm2 ($+12\%$) and Electricity ($+13\%$), indicating the optimal architecture is dataset-dependent. FiLM remains consistently worst ($+48$--$147\%$), confirming that re-injecting only $(\mu,\sigma)$ is insufficient---the experts need access to the full raw signal, not just the stripped statistics.
