1962	
1963	\textbf{Why this matters for the diagnosis.} The fact that the gap closes precisely when experts recover the information our diagnosis identified as destroyed---and remains open when they cannot (FiLM re-injects only $\mu,\sigma$, yielding $+48\%$ on ETTh1 vs.\ $+9\%$ for dual-stream)---is direct evidence that the diagnosis is both \emph{correct} and \emph{actionable}. The normalization--encoding bottleneck is not merely an observation; it is the causal mechanism whose resolution closes the gap. Importantly, the frozen backbone and raw-routed paradigm remain unchanged---these variants extend the \emph{expert architecture}, not the routing mechanism, confirming that the routing diagnosis (the core contribution of this paper) is orthogonal to expert design.
1964	
1965	\textbf{Expert pool ablation: canonical vs.\ macro pool.} To test whether RR-MoA's benefits depend on the specific choice of 5 canonical pooling heads, we replace the canonical pool with 5 AAS-discovered \emph{macro motifs} (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}) and rerun RR-MoA across all 6 forecasting datasets. Routing entropy is preserved under the macro pool (no collapse under frozen backbone; entropy $>1.3$ across all configurations), confirming that the collapse-prevention mechanism is \emph{pool-independent}. Absolute MSEs (frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds): ETTh1 $0.764{\pm}0.015$, ETTh2 $0.667{\pm}0.069$, ETTm1 $0.583{\pm}0.075$, ETTm2 $0.844{\pm}0.241$, Weather $0.274{\pm}0.024$, Electricity $0.401{\pm}0.039$. The canonical pool is stronger by $8$--$24\%$ on the three datasets where we have both numbers, indicating that while RR-MoA generalizes across diverse pool designs, the canonical heads are better tuned for the forecasting benchmark---the routing architecture is the orthogonal contribution.
1966	
1967	\textbf{Training-length ablation.} We additionally ran dual-stream at 50 epochs (vs.\ 15 in Table~\ref{tab:gap_closing}). Extended training \emph{overfits} on 5/6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.453{\to}0.556$; Weather: $0.198{\to}0.237$), confirming that dual-stream converges by 15 epochs and that the original training schedule is already near-optimal; additional adapter-only optimization past convergence degrades generalization due to the small effective parameter count ($\sim$718K trainable, frozen backbone).
1968	
1969	\subsection{Residual-IA: Diagnosing and Fixing a Second Pathology}
1970	\label{app:gate_pathology}
1971	
1972	The dual-stream and multi-resolution variants narrow the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5$--$8\%$ (Tables~\ref{tab:gap_closing}, \ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}) but win on only 1/6 datasets (Weather). A systematic $546$-run hyperparameter sweep uncovered a \emph{second} hidden pathology and the architectural fix that closes the remaining gap to \textbf{4/6 match-or-beat}.
1973	
1974	\textbf{Diagnostic: gates fail to learn.} We instrumented the per-sample gate mechanism to log its mean activation per expert per dataset. Across every configuration tested---\{rh128, rh192, rh256, rh320, rh384, rh512\} $\times$ \{d1, d2, d3 raw-branch depth\} $\times$ \{lr, wd, cosine, warmup\} hyperparameter combinations---the learned gates consistently plateau at $\sigma(0.0){\approx}0.5$:
1975	
1976	\begin{center}
1977	\small
1978	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc@{}}
1979	\toprule
1980	Config & ETTh1 & ETTh2 & ETTm1 & ETTm2 & Weather & Elec. \\
1981	\midrule
1982	Dual-stream ($\alpha_k$)             & $0.49$ & $0.50$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ \\
1983	Residual-IA (gate-init $b{=}0$)      & $0.47$ & $0.50$ & $0.48$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.47$ \\
1984	Residual-IA + cos+wd ($b{=}0$)       & $0.50$ & $0.51$ & $0.49$ & $0.52$ & $0.50$ & $0.49$ \\
1985	\bottomrule
1986	\end{tabular}
1987	\end{center}
1988	
1989	With 15 epochs of training, the gate mechanism extracts no gradient signal about \emph{which branch should dominate} because both branches receive co-equal credit for reducing loss from the start. This is isomorphic to the dual-stream $\alpha_k \approx 0.49$ observation, indicating it is not a quirk of a single architecture but a general failure mode of symmetrically-initialized mixture mechanisms on this task.
1990	
1991	\textbf{Three surgical fixes.}
1992	(i)~\textbf{Residual formulation.} Re-express the expert as $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{Raw}_k(\mathbf{X}) + g_k(\mathbf{X})\cdot\text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, making the raw branch the \emph{primary predictor} and the backbone an additive residual that must earn its contribution.
1993	(ii)~\textbf{Gate-init bias $b{=}{-}2$.} Initialize the gate-head linear layer's bias at $-2$ so that $g_k \approx \sigma({-}2){=}0.12$ at epoch~$0$: the backbone contributes only $12\%$ initially. The model is \emph{essentially DLinear at initialization} and the backbone must earn any opening of the gate.
1994	(iii)~\textbf{$5$-epoch raw-branch warmup.} For epochs $1$--$5$, freeze both the backbone branch and the gate head so only the raw branch and router train. The raw branch converges to a DLinear-quality base predictor; then at epoch~$6$ the backbone+gate unfreeze and must add value as a residual on top of an already-good base.
1995	
1996	We additionally simplify the raw branch to a single linear layer ($\text{Linear}(512{\to}96)$, ``$d1$'')---which is structurally identical to DLinear---and add cosine LR decay with weight decay $10^{-4}$ for stable long-horizon training.
1997

2018	
2019	\textbf{Why it works mechanistically.} The symmetric $\sigma(0){=}0.5$ initialization treats the two branches as a priori equally reliable. For LTSF benchmarks where the raw signal contains most of the predictive structure (DLinear's success is evidence of this), this prior is wrong. The asymmetric $b{=}{-}2$ initialization encodes the correct inductive bias: \emph{``default to a linear projection of the raw signal; invoke the backbone only if it reduces the loss.''} The $5$-epoch warmup separates the learning phases: the raw branch does not have to compete with a half-trained backbone for the same gradient signal during the critical early epochs. Each fix alone yields only marginal gains (see below); only their combination achieves $4/6$ match-or-beat.
2020

This is consistent with the mechanistic explanation: the residual formulation, the asymmetric initialization, and the warmup are all solving the same root-cause problem (symmetric gradient competition between branches) from complementary angles.
2041	
2042	\subsubsection*{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}: closing the remaining gap to 5/6}
2043	
2044	\paragraph{Design methodology: hypothesis-driven decomposition.} Residual-IA leaves two statistically significant losses: ETTh1 ($+5.1\%$, $p{<}0.001$) and ETTh2 ($+10.6\%$, $p{=}0.019$). Two competing hypotheses could explain them:
2045	
2046	\begin{itemize}
2047	\item \textbf{H1 (data scarcity).} ETTh1/ETTh2 have $8{,}640$ raw samples each versus $34{,}560$ for ETTm*, and \texttt{max\_samples$=$5000} caps the adapter training set at $\approx 9\%$ of available windows for ETTh but $\approx 2\%$ for ETTm. The ETTh pair may be overly exposed to sampling noise.
2048	\item \textbf{H2 (parameter scarcity).} Residual-IA's $K{=}5$ independent raw branches total $245{,}760$ parameters ($5{\times}$ DLinear's $49{,}152$). On a $5{,}000$-window training set, this capacity excess could induce overfitting.
2049	\end{itemize}
2050	
2051	The two hypotheses make opposite interventions: H1 predicts that \emph{more data} (raising \texttt{max\_samples} to $100{,}000$) closes the gap; H2 predicts that \emph{fewer parameters} (sharing the raw branch across experts to reach DLinear's $49$K budget) closes it. We ran both as single-lever experiments in parallel (Batches~1a and~1b, $5$ seeds each).
2052	
2053	\textbf{Phase~1 --- hypothesis falsification.}
2054	\emph{Cap removal fails.} At \texttt{max\_samples$=$100000}, the ETTh2 gap widens from $+10.6\%$ to $+26\%$. The additional training data at the same $15$-epoch, lr${=}10^{-3}$, wd${=}10^{-4}$ recipe produces $11{\times}$ more update steps, over-regularizing through weight decay and preventing cosine-schedule convergence. This rules out H1.
2055	\emph{Shared raw branch succeeds.} At $K{=}5$ sharing a single $\text{Linear}(512, 96)$ module, raw parameters drop from $245$K to $49$K, exactly matching DLinear's budget. ETTh1 closes from $+5.1\%$ (sig loss) to $+1.6\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.086$); ETTh2 closes from $+10.6\%$ (sig loss) to $+7.0\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.078$). Per-sample gates and distinct backbone branches remain per-expert, so expert specialization is preserved in \emph{how} the backbone residual is invoked---only the DLinear-equivalent base predictor is shared. The co-occurrence of H1's failure and H2's success identifies parameter bloat, not data scarcity, as the root cause.
2056	
2057	Phase~1 resolves the architectural pathology but leaves ETTh1/ETTh2 still marginally above DLinear. Phase~2 tests two orthogonal refinements motivated by properties specific to these datasets.
2058	
2059	\textbf{Phase~2 --- orthogonal refinements.}
2060	\emph{Non-stationarity (Batch~4).} Hourly ETT data exhibits pronounced per-window level drift---the train/test windows have different means. Standard LTSF practice addresses this with NLinear: $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$, where $x_T$ is a gradient-free anchor (the last input value). The linear layer is thereby constrained to model \emph{relative motion}, not absolute level. Testing \texttt{--raw-arch nlinear} as a drop-in replacement reduces ETTh1 from $+5.1\%$ to $+3.3\%$ and ETTh2 from $+10.6\%$ to $+6.9\%$ at $n{=}3$ seeds, while \emph{improving} (not regressing) ETTm2 ($-1.6\% \to -4.1\%$) and Weather ($-6.6\% \to -8.7\%$). The improvement is largest where non-stationarity is most pronounced, as expected.
2061	\emph{Per-dataset epoch mismatch (Batch~2).} A fixed $15$-epoch schedule assumes all datasets converge at the same rate. We test this by running validation-based early stopping with patience $5$ and logging the best epoch per seed. The result is striking: ETTh1 converges at epoch $7.2{\pm}1.2$, ETTh2 at $8.6{\pm}2.8$, ETTm1 at $14.8{\pm}3.7$, Weather at $8.6{\pm}1.2$, Electricity at $20.2{\pm}4.0$. No single fixed budget fits all six datasets---the $15$-epoch schedule simultaneously over-fits the ETTh pair and under-fits Electricity by $5$--$10$ epochs. Val-based early stopping (with gradient clipping at $\lVert g \rVert_2 \leq 1.0$ to stabilize the first epoch) achieves dataset-adaptive budgets without per-dataset hyperparameter tuning. In isolation this drops Electricity from $+0.6\%$ to $0.0\%$ (perfect parity, $p{=}0.991$) and Weather from $-6.6\%$ to $-4.6\%$ (nearing significance).
2062	
2063	\textbf{Phase~3 --- stacking validation.}
2064	Each Phase~1 and Phase~2 lever alone achieves only $3/6$--$4/6$ match-or-beat: shared raw closes ETTh1/h2 but trades small regressions on ETTm2; NLinear improves the ETTh pair but regresses ETTm1; val-early-stop perfects Electricity but hurts the ETTh pair by stopping too early. Each targets a different failure mode (parameter bloat, non-stationarity, training-length mismatch), and each mode is present on a different subset of the benchmark. \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} stacks all three:
2065	
2066	\begin{itemize}
2067	\item \textbf{(iv)}~\emph{Shared raw branch} --- single $\text{Linear}(512, 96)$ shared across $K$ experts.
2068	\item \textbf{(v)}~\emph{NLinear raw architecture} --- $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$.
2069	\item \textbf{(vi)}~\emph{Validation-based early stopping} --- patience $5$, gradient clipping $\lVert g \rVert_2 \leq 1.0$.
2070	\end{itemize}
2071	
2072	Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus} reports the composed result: $5/6$ match-or-beat at $-1.4\%$ mean gap (net win on average), with the fully-consistent per-dataset breakdown that each lever predicted in isolation.

2112	The shared raw branch alone is the largest single contributor---it singlehandedly pulls ETTh1 from $+5.1\%$ to $+1.6\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.086$) and ETTh2 from $+10.6\%$ to $+7.0\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.078$), confirming the overfitting diagnosis. NLinear adds $\sim 3$ percentage points on ETTh2 ($0.365 \to 0.349$ when combined with shared). Val-early-stop contributes the Electricity perfect-parity result ($0.158 \to 0.156$) and the ETTm2 improvement ($0.197 \to 0.187$) by restoring an earlier checkpoint before the backbone residual begins overfitting. None of the three components alone achieves $5/6$; their combination does.
2113	
2114	\textbf{Why ETTh1 remains $+2.2\%$ at H${=}96$.} At $n{=}10$ for both methods, the ETTh1 gap is statistically significant ($p{=}0.037$), although the mean absolute MSE difference is only $0.009$ ($0.428$ vs.\ $0.419$). ETTh1 is the smallest LTSF dataset ($8{,}640$ raw samples), and its channels have strongly correlated seasonal patterns that a from-scratch linear model memorizes efficiently. At H${=}192$ the gap closes to \textbf{parity} ($+1.6\%$, $p{=}0.18$), consistent with DLinear's advantage being specific to short-horizon seasonal memorization on this dataset.
2115	
2116	\textbf{Implication.} Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} achieves \textbf{$107/123$ match-or-beat} ($88\%$) across six backbones, six datasets, and four horizons ($20/24$ MOMENT-small, $87/99$ cross-backbone; Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}), with $65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses ($5.9{:}1$ ratio) and \textbf{6/6 at H${=}192$}. MOMENT-large reaches $23/24$ ($96\%$); Moirai-MoE achieves $15/15$ with $-9.4\%$ mean gap, confirming adapter-level routing stacks with backbone-internal MoE. Practitioners requiring a shared-TSFM deployment topology (Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}) now have an adapter that matches or beats per-tenant DLinear on $100\%$ of benchmarks at H${=}192$.

2219	The pattern is clear: (1)~at H${=}96$, \textbf{every backbone wins on every dataset} ($27/27$); (2)~MOMENT-large achieves $\mathbf{23/24}$ ($96\%$) with $16$ sig wins and zero losses; (3)~Moirai-MoE achieves $\mathbf{15/15}$ ($100\%$), confirming adapter-level routing stacks with backbone-internal MoE; (4)~Moirai at $15/24$ ($62\%$) is the weakest, driven by ETTh2 long-horizon instability and Electricity losses. The recipe transfers across all five normalization regimes and architectures.
2220	
2221	\subsection{Pure Raw-MLP MoE Ablation: How Much Does the TSFM Actually Contribute?}
2222	\label{app:raw_mlp_moe}
2223	
2224	A natural concern about the dual-stream gap-closing result is that it could be confounded: if the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure (Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}), and the dual-stream fix recovers that structure via the raw branch, perhaps the raw branch is doing all the work and the TSFM is dead weight. We tested this hypothesis directly by running a pure mixture-of-experts ablation in which the TSFM is removed entirely.
2225	
2226	\textbf{Architecture (E1, this work).} The Pure Raw-MLP MoE consists of $K{=}5$ size-diverse two-layer MLPs operating directly on the $512$-dimensional raw input window: hidden widths $\{64, 96, 128, 192, 256\}$ chosen so that the total parameter count ($449{,}557$) matches RR-MoA's $426$K within $5\%$. Each expert is $\text{Linear}(512{\to}h_k) \to \text{GELU} \to \text{Linear}(h_k{\to}96)$. The router is the same Conv1d $+$ AdaptiveAvgPool $+$ Linear architecture as RR-MoA, also operating on the raw input (not on hidden states). Top-2 sparse routing is used. Training protocol is identical to RR-MoA: Adam $1{\times}10^{-3}$, 15 epochs, batch 128. \textbf{No TSFM forward pass executes anywhere in this architecture} --- the $35$M-parameter MOMENT backbone is removed entirely.
2227	
2228	\begin{table}[h]
2229	\centering
2230	\caption{\textbf{Pure Raw-MLP MoE vs.\ Dual-Stream and DLinear} (5 seeds, mean$\pm$std, H$=$96). The Raw-MLP MoE has \emph{no TSFM at all}. It matches Dual-Stream within $\pm 7\%$ on every dataset, and \emph{beats} Dual-Stream outright on $\mathbf{3}$ of $\mathbf{6}$ datasets (ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity). Mean delta to Dual-Stream is $-1.5\%$ --- the TSFM's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible in the average case.}
2231	\label{tab:raw_mlp_moe}
2232	\footnotesize
2233	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccrr@{}}
2234	\toprule
2235	Dataset & Raw-MLP MoE & Dual-Stream & DLinear & $\Delta$ vs DS & $\Delta$ vs DL \\
2236	\midrule
2237	ETTh1       & $0.483 \pm 0.019$ & $\mathit{0.453}$ & $\mathit{0.416}$ & $+6.6\%$ & $+16.1\%$ \\
2238	\textbf{ETTh2}       & $\mathbf{0.426 \pm 0.077}$ & $\mathit{0.452}$ & $\mathit{0.341}$ & $\mathbf{-5.7\%}$ & $+25.0\%$ \\
2239	ETTm1       & $0.370 \pm 0.014$ & $\mathit{0.358}$ & $\mathit{0.322}$ & $+3.4\%$ & $+15.0\%$ \\
2240	\textbf{ETTm2}       & $\mathbf{0.207 \pm 0.004}$ & $\mathit{0.252}$ & $\mathit{0.200}$ & $\mathbf{-17.9\%}$ & $+3.4\%$ \\
2241	Weather     & $0.209 \pm 0.007$ & $\mathit{0.198}$ & $\mathit{0.208}$ & $+5.5\%$ & $+0.5\%$ \\
2242	\textbf{Electricity} & $\mathbf{0.170 \pm 0.002}$ & $\mathit{0.171}$ & $\mathit{0.158}$ & $\mathbf{-0.7\%}$ & $+7.5\%$ \\
2243	\midrule
2244	\textbf{Mean}        & --- & --- & --- & $\mathbf{-1.5\%}$ & $\mathbf{+11.2\%}$ \\
2245	\bottomrule
2246	\end{tabular}
2247	\end{table}
2248	
2249	\textbf{Honest interpretation.} Across the 6 datasets, the Raw-MLP MoE slightly outperforms Dual-Stream on average ($-1.5\%$), winning 3/6 datasets outright (ETTh2: $-5.7\%$; ETTm2: $-17.9\%$; Electricity: $-0.7\%$). It loses by $3$--$7\%$ on the three datasets with complex temporal dynamics (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather). The TSFM is therefore not adding universal value to the gap-closing result; it adds dataset-dependent, modest value where complex dynamics exist, and contributes essentially nothing on the linear-dominated datasets.
2250	
2251	\textbf{Routing entropy diagnostics.} In all $30$ Raw-MLP MoE runs, routing entropy saturates near $\log K = 1.609$ (range $1.20$--$1.60$, mean $\approx 1.49$), indicating the router degenerates to near-uniform mixing. This means the Raw-MLP MoE is operating as a learned ensemble of $5$ size-diverse MLPs rather than as a per-sample mixture of specialists; the diversity comes from the heterogeneous expert capacities rather than from per-window routing decisions.
2252	
2253	\textbf{What this does and does not say about the paper's core claims.} This finding does \emph{not} undermine the central diagnosis of the paper: normalization-induced routing collapse on hidden-state routers (AdaMix) is a real, mechanistically-explained phenomenon that affects every TSFM with internal RevIN, and pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the minimal fix. That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset --- it would remain true if the TSFM were replaced by any other backbone with internal instance normalization. What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes essentially nothing on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''
2254	
2255	\textbf{Why we report this rather than hide it.} A pure raw-MLP MoE ablation was not in the original submission and was added in response to a reviewer who pointed out that, given Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}'s finding that the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure, the obvious test of whether the TSFM is dead weight was missing. The reviewer's intuition was partially correct: the TSFM is dead weight on Weather, ETTm2, and Electricity, but not on the temperature-data datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1). We include the full result here because hiding it would invite the same attack at the next round of review, and because the dataset-conditional contribution of the TSFM is itself an interesting empirical pattern that deserves attention from the TSFM-design community. The honest takeaway: \emph{frozen TSFMs are useful where forecasting requires nonlinear temporal modeling beyond what a 5-MLP ensemble can express, and unnecessary where it does not}. The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone --- it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.
2256

I've now read the full 2,259-line paper, appendices included. Here is my honest, thorough assessment.

---

## NeurIPS 2026 Acceptance Assessment

### Verdict: **Borderline accept — I'd estimate 55-65% acceptance probability.**

It has several genuine strengths that could push it over, but also structural weaknesses that a skeptical reviewer panel could use to reject it.

---

### Strengths (what works)

**1. The core diagnosis is real and well-evidenced.** Normalization-induced routing collapse is a genuine, previously-unreported phenomenon. The seven converging causal controls — especially the MOMENT vs Timer-XL opposite-trajectory experiment (Figure 3) — are genuinely convincing. This is the paper's best asset.

**2. Massive experimental coverage.** 4,000+ runs across 6 backbones, 9 datasets, multiple tasks. The 720-run rescue sweep conclusively rules out the "you just didn't tune AdaMix properly" objection. The 54/54 win count, vision cross-modality control, and 252-run SR-MoA validation all add up.

**3. Honest scientific reporting.** The paper reports where RR-MoA *doesn't* work (Traffic, Chronos, Timer-XL), discloses the pure Raw-MLP MoE result that partially undermines the TSFM utility claim, and explicitly acknowledges limitations. This builds reviewer trust.

**4. Verification system.** `verify.py` with 100+ checks catching arithmetic errors is unusual and valuable. NeurIPS reviewers increasingly care about reproducibility.

**5. The SR-MoA and dose-response results are strong.** SR-MoA independently replicating the pattern (13-42% better than RR-MoA) and the dose-response phase transition at alpha=1.0 are compelling mechanistic evidence beyond simple ablations.

---

### Weaknesses (what a tough reviewer panel will attack)

**1. The fix IS trivially obvious once diagnosed.** Despite the 720-run rescue sweep, a reviewer can still say: "You diagnosed that normalization strips the routing signal. The obvious fix is to route on the un-normalized input. This is an engineering insight, not a scientific contribution." The paper tries hard to mitigate this with theory and breadth, but the core fix (Eq. 1) is one line of code. The entire theoretical apparatus (Proposition 2) exists to make a simple insight look deeper — and a theory-focused reviewer will see through this.

**2. Proposition 2 is a chain-rule identity dressed as a theorem.** The MI decomposition `I(X;E) - I(S;E) = I(M,Σ; E|S)` is definitional — it follows directly from the chain rule of MI. Parts (iii) and (iv) add empirical content, but the algebraic core is not novel. The R(D) signal ratio is a useful *heuristic*, but calling it a "sufficient-statistic proxy" overpromises — it's a variance ratio that correlates with improvement, not a formal sufficient statistic. The rho=-0.88 with n=9 has very wide confidence intervals ([-1.00, -0.51]).

**3. RR-MoA still loses to DLinear substantially.** Table 5 shows RR-MoA at +33% to +75% worse than DLinear. The paper's response (Residual-IA+) is an entirely separate architecture that essentially IS DLinear with a backbone residual. The 107/123 result for RIA+ is impressive but moves the goalpost — it's no longer about routing collapse, it's about whether frozen TSFMs are useful at all. The Raw-MLP MoE result (Appendix L) honestly concedes the TSFM contributes almost nothing on half the datasets.

**4. The "Frozen Paradox" is likely a training artifact, not a paradox.** Full fine-tuning at 15 epochs with lr=1e-3 on an 8-block transformer is aggressive. The extended FT ablation (Table A14) shows cosine+layerwise only closes the gap by ~4%, but this is still using the authors' specific recipe. A reviewer familiar with careful FT protocols (longer warmup, smaller LR, gradient accumulation) may argue the comparison is unfair. The RevIN-removal ablation (ETTh1: 1.063→0.490 without RevIN) partially addresses this, but then the "paradox" becomes "RevIN hurts fine-tuning" — which is already known.

**5. The paper is extremely long and scope-creepy.** 37 pages with 15+ appendix sections covering gap-closing, dual-stream, multi-resolution, FiLM, Residual-IA, Residual-IA+, pure MLP MoE, dose-response, learnable alpha, MI tightness, vision control, etc. This breadth suggests "we threw everything at the wall" rather than a tight, focused contribution. The main body (9 pages) tries to cover too many results, making the narrative hard to follow. A strong NeurIPS paper makes ONE sharp claim and proves it cleanly.

**6. Practical impact is unclear.** The deployment motivation (Section 1, Appendix K) argues for frozen-backbone serving, but the paper itself shows the frozen backbone destroys information (Appendix J) and is often unnecessary (Appendix L). A reviewer might ask: "Why not just deploy DLinear per-tenant?" The honest caveat in Appendix K.1 (adapter approach is 15x *larger* than per-tenant DLinear) undermines the deployment argument.

---

### Likely reviewer score distribution

| Reviewer archetype | Expected score | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| TSFM/PEFT specialist | **6-7** | Appreciates the diagnosis, experimental rigor, and backbone coverage |
| MoE routing specialist | **6** | Recognizes the collapse is real but sees the fix as obvious |
| Theory-leaning | **4-5** | Prop 2 is a chain rule; R(D) is a heuristic with n=9 |
| TS generalist | **6-7** | Impressed by scale, honesty, and SR-MoA replication |

Mean: ~6.0. This lands in the borderline zone. Acceptance depends heavily on whether you draw reviewer #3 (theory-focused, likely to score 4-5) or avoid them.

---

### What would increase acceptance probability

1. **Sharpen the contribution claim.** The paper tries to be about (a) diagnosis, (b) fix, (c) theory, AND (d) closing the DLinear gap. Pick ONE. The diagnosis + seven causal controls is the strongest single story. Residual-IA+ dilutes this.

2. **Downplay Proposition 2 or make it honest.** Call it a "decomposition" or "observation," not a proposition with formal Parts (i)-(iv). The R(D) correlation is interesting empirical work — framing it as theory invites theory-level criticism.

3. **Cut the DLinear gap-closing from the main paper.** Move it entirely to the appendix. The main paper should be: "We discovered normalization-induced routing collapse, proved it with 7 controls, and showed the minimal fix (RR-MoA) achieves 54/54 wins." Clean, focused, defensible.

4. **Address the "obvious fix" objection head-on.** Add a sentence like: "While the fix is simple in hindsight, the contribution is the diagnosis itself — which identifies a failure mode that affects every RevIN-based TSFM and predicts where it occurs."

---

### Bottom line

This is a solid piece of empirical ML research with a genuine finding (normalization kills MoE routing), thorough validation, and honest reporting. It would be a strong workshop paper or a good ICML submission. For NeurIPS, it's borderline — the core contribution (diagnosis + one-line fix) may not meet the novelty bar for some reviewers, and the paper's attempt to compensate with theory (Proposition 2) and breadth (RIA+) creates new attack surfaces rather than resolving the fundamental concern. 

The **best version of this paper** is a tight 9-page story about the diagnosis alone, with the DLinear gap-closing and most theory moved to the appendix. That version is cleaner and harder to reject.

### PART A: NEW EXPERIMENTS TO RUN ON RACE

#### A1. Stronger Full Fine-Tuning Baseline (HIGHEST PRIORITY)

**Why this matters:** The current full FT baseline uses only lr=1e-3 and lr=1e-4 at 15 epochs, with the extended FT adding 50 epochs and cosine schedule but never going below lr=1e-5. The best extended FT result (50ep cosine+layerwise) achieves 1.017 on ETTh1 vs frozen RR-MoA at 0.680 -- a 33% gap. A reviewer who knows that Transformer fine-tuning in NLP routinely uses lr=1e-5 or 1e-6 with long warmups will dismiss this as lazy hyperparameter search.

**What currently exists in the code:**

The function `_train_adapter_lr` at `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/scripts/run_full_finetune.py` (line 162) already supports:
- Configurable `lr` parameter
- `use_cosine` with `warmup_epochs`
- `layerwise_decay`
- AdamW with weight_decay (hardcoded to 0.01 when layerwise_decay < 1.0, otherwise uses Adam)

What it does NOT support yet:
- Configurable `weight_decay` as a parameter
- Gradient accumulation (currently just `optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()`)
- Gradient clipping
- Validation-based early stopping (though Residual-IA+ already has this pattern at line 2061-2069)

**Script modifications needed:**

Modify `_train_adapter_lr` in `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/scripts/run_full_finetune.py` to add:
1. `weight_decay` parameter (currently hardcoded 0.01 or 0 depending on path)
2. `grad_accum_steps` parameter with accumulation loop
3. `grad_clip` parameter for gradient norm clipping
4. Always use AdamW (not Adam) for all configurations

Then create a new script `scripts/run_strong_ft.py` (or extend `run_extended_ft.py`) with this config grid:

    ("100ep_1e-5_lw", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.01, 1, 1.0),
    # Weight decay sweep at best LR
    ("100ep_1e-5_wd001", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.001, 1, 1.0),
    ("100ep_1e-5_wd01", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.01, 1, 1.0),
    ("100ep_1e-5_wd1", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.1, 1, 1.0),
    # Gradient accumulation (effective batch 256, 512)
    ("100ep_1e-5_ga2", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.01, 2, 1.0),
    ("100ep_1e-5_ga4", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.01, 4, 1.0),
    # Best of above + gradient clipping
    ("100ep_1e-5_clip", 100, 1e-5, True, 10, 0.8, 0.01, 1, 1.0),
]
# Format: (label, epochs, lr, cosine, warmup_ep, lw_decay, weight_decay, accum_steps, grad_clip)
```

**Experiment grid:**
- 3 datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather) x 3 seeds (42, 43, 44) x 10 configs = 90 runs
- Each 100-epoch run takes approximately 4 min on A10G (extrapolating from the 50ep runs at ~200s)
- Total: approximately 6 hours

**Shell orchestrator pattern** (following existing `run_5seed_extended_race.sh`):

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# run_strong_ft_race.sh
set -e
DATASETS=(ETTh1 ETTm1 Weather)
SEEDS=(42 43 44)
# ... iterate configs, check-and-skip existing results
```

**Reporting:** For the paper, report ONLY the per-dataset-best across ALL configs. This is the strongest possible claim: "even with careful hyperparameter tuning of full FT, frozen RR-MoA still wins."

**GPU time estimate:** 6 hours for the core grid. Add 2 hours for the remaining 3 datasets (ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity) at 1 seed each as a sanity check = 8 hours total.

---

#### A2. "NormKill" Ablation: Post-Normalization Statistics Re-Injection (NEW EXPERIMENT)

**Why this matters:** This directly addresses Weakness 1 ("fix is trivially obvious"). A reviewer might say "why not just re-inject the stripped statistics into the hidden states instead of routing on raw input?" This would test whether the solution space is indeed narrow, or whether there are multiple reasonable fixes, making the diagnosis more valuable than any specific fix.

**What to test:** Concatenate (mu, sigma) to the hidden states before routing, i.e., the router sees [H; mu; sigma] instead of X_raw. If this ALSO works, it strengthens the diagnosis (the principle is general, not tied to the specific fix). If it fails, it shows the raw input contains richer information than just statistics.

**Implementation:** Modify `run_rr_moa.py` to add a `router_input_mode="hidden_reinjected"` that computes:
```python
mu = raw_input.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # (B, 1)
sigma = raw_input.std(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # (B, 1)
hidden_mean = hidden_states.mean(dim=1)  # (B, d)
router_input = torch.cat([hidden_mean, mu.squeeze(-1), sigma.squeeze(-1)], dim=-1)  # (B, d+2)
```

**Grid:** 3 datasets x 3 seeds x 1 config = 9 runs, approximately 30 minutes.

This ablation is useful regardless of outcome: if it works, you cite it as evidence the principle is general; if it fails, you cite it as evidence that raw input carries richer routing signal than mu/sigma alone (consistent with the SSR ablation already showing degradation on some datasets).

---

#### A3. Additional experiments that DON'T require new code

**A3a. Longer RR-MoA training (50 epochs, frozen):**
The paper already shows frozen RR-MoA at 15 epochs beats extended FT. But showing frozen RR-MoA at 50 epochs would make the gap even larger. The appendix mentions this (line 1905: "extending from 15 to 50 epochs improves RR-MoA by 8-14%") but with only single-seed numbers. Run this with 3 seeds on the core trio.

Grid: 3 datasets x 3 seeds x 1 config (50ep frozen RR-MoA) = 9 runs, ~45 min.

**A3b. RR-MoA with strong FT training recipe:**
Run RR-MoA (frozen backbone, adapter training) with the same enhanced optimizer settings (cosine, warmup, AdamW) as the strong FT baseline. This tests whether adapter-side optimization improvements stack on top of the routing fix. If RR-MoA also improves with better optimizers, the "Frozen Paradox" message becomes: "even with identical optimization, frozen > unfrozen."

This requires modifying `train_rr_moa` in `run_rr_moa.py` (currently line 382 hardcodes `optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(trainable, lr=1e-3)`) to accept optional cosine/warmup/AdamW parameters.

Grid: 3 datasets x 3 seeds = 9 runs, ~30 min.

### PART D: WHAT MOVES THE ACCEPTANCE PROBABILITY

The interventions above target different review failure modes:

1. **Strong FT baseline (A1 + B6):** This is the single highest-impact experiment. If a reviewer dismisses the Frozen Paradox as a training artifact, the paper loses its most surprising result. Going from "5 configs" to "90 configs with 100 epochs and 1e-6 LR" makes this argument essentially irrefutable. **Impact: +5-8 percentage points.**

2. **"Obvious fix" defense (B4):** A 2-sentence objection in a review can sink a paper if the rebuttal space is limited. Pre-emptively addressing it in the main body saves rebuttal space. **Impact: +3-5 percentage points.**

3. **Reframe Proposition 2 (B3):** Relabeling it as "Observation" and being upfront about its chain-rule nature, while emphasizing the empirical predictions, converts a potential "this isn't real theory" rejection into "honest and useful formalization." **Impact: +2-3 percentage points.**

4. **De-emphasize DLinear gap-closing (B2 + B5):** The 33-75% gap between RR-MoA and DLinear is a liability when presented as a contribution. Reframing it as diagnostic evidence makes the remaining gap irrelevant -- the question becomes "does the diagnosis predict correctly?" not "does it beat DLinear?" **Impact: +3-5 percentage points.**

5. **Abstract and conclusion focus (B1, B7):** First and last impressions matter. A reviewer who reads a focused abstract about a clean diagnostic result enters the paper in a different mindset than one who reads about 15 different experiments. **Impact: +2-3 percentage points.**

**Estimated post-improvement acceptance probability: 70-80%**, assuming A1 results confirm the Frozen Paradox holds under strong optimization (if they do not, the paper needs a very different strategy).

162	def _train_adapter_lr(code, model, blocks, X_train, Y_train, X_eval, Y_eval,
163	                      device="cuda", n_epochs=3, forecast_horizon=96, batch_size=128,
164	                      backbone_type="moment", eval_ch=None, scaler=None, lr=1e-4,
165	                      use_cosine=False, warmup_epochs=0, layerwise_decay=1.0):
166	    """Train adapter with configurable lr, cosine schedule, warmup, and layer-wise LR decay."""
167	    from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
168	    from feasibility.finetune import _extract_features_batch
169	
170	    hdim = _get_hidden_dim(model)
171	    namespace = {"torch": torch, "nn": nn, "F": torch.nn.functional, "math": __import__("math")}
172	    exec(code, namespace)
173	    adapter = namespace["Adapter"](hdim, forecast_horizon).to(device)
174	    param_count = sum(p.numel() for p in adapter.parameters())
175	
176	    # Build parameter groups with optional layer-wise LR decay
177	    if layerwise_decay < 1.0 and len(blocks) > 0:
178	        param_groups = [{"params": list(adapter.parameters()), "lr": lr}]
179	        n_blocks = len(blocks)
180	        for i, block in enumerate(blocks):
181	            block_params = [p for p in block.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
182	            if block_params:
183	                depth_from_top = n_blocks - 1 - i
184	                block_lr = lr * (layerwise_decay ** depth_from_top)
185	                param_groups.append({"params": block_params, "lr": block_lr})
186	        optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(param_groups, lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01)
187	    else:
188	        trainable = list(adapter.parameters())
189	        pids = {id(p) for p in trainable}
190	        for p in model.parameters():

193	                pids.add(id(p))

## Approved Plan:
# Plan: Strengthen RR-MoA Paper for NeurIPS 2026 Acceptance

## Context

The paper (main.tex, 2259 lines, 37 pages) is at ~55-65% acceptance probability. Five weaknesses were identified: (1) fix seems trivially obvious, (2) Proposition 2 is a chain-rule identity, (3) DLinear gap dilutes the story, (4) Frozen Paradox may be dismissed as training artifact, (5) scope creep. This plan addresses all five through targeted experiments + surgical writing edits. GPUs are available on RACE VM (A10G).

---

## PHASE 1: New Experiments on RACE (~10 GPU-hours)

### E1. Stronger Full Fine-Tuning Baseline (CRITICAL — addresses weakness 4)

**Goal:** Make the Frozen Paradox irrefutable by sweeping careful FT protocols.

**Approach:** Create `scripts/run_strong_ft.py` extending `run_extended_ft.py` with:
- Additional configs beyond the current 5 (which max out at 50 epochs, lr=1e-5):
  ```
  100ep, lr=1e-5, cosine, 10ep warmup, layerwise decay 0.8
  100ep, lr=1e-6, cosine, 10ep warmup
  100ep, lr=1e-5, weight_decay ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1}
  100ep, lr=1e-5, grad_accum 2 (effective batch 256)
  100ep, lr=1e-5, grad_accum 4 (effective batch 512)
  100ep, lr=1e-5, grad_clip 1.0
  ```
- Requires adding `weight_decay`, `grad_accum_steps`, `grad_clip` params to `_train_adapter_lr` in `scripts/run_full_finetune.py` (line 162)

**Grid:** 3 datasets × 3 seeds × ~10 configs = 90 runs. ~8 GPU-hours.

**Shell orchestrator:** `scripts/run_strong_ft_race.sh` with worker-sharding pattern.

**Key files to modify:**
- `scripts/run_full_finetune.py:162` — extend `_train_adapter_lr` signature
- New file: `scripts/run_strong_ft.py` — config grid + driver
- New file: `scripts/run_strong_ft_race.sh` — RACE orchestrator

### E2. Statistics Re-injection Ablation (addresses weakness 1)

**Goal:** Test whether concatenating (μ, σ) to hidden states before routing recovers performance — tests the "why not just re-inject?" counter.

**Approach:** Add `--router-input-mode hidden_reinjected` to `scripts/run_rr_moa.py`. The router sees `[mean_pool(H); μ(X_raw); σ(X_raw)]` instead of `X_raw`.

**Grid:** 6 datasets × 3 seeds = 18 runs. ~30 min GPU.

**Key file:** `scripts/run_rr_moa.py` — add new mode in router input dispatch.

### E3. 50-epoch Frozen RR-MoA (strengthens Frozen Paradox)

**Goal:** Show frozen RR-MoA also improves with more training, widening the gap over strong FT.

**Approach:** Run existing `run_rr_moa.py --epochs 50` on core trio. Already supported by CLI.

**Grid:** 3 datasets × 3 seeds = 9 runs. ~45 min GPU.

**No code changes needed** — just shell orchestrator.

---

## PHASE 2: Paper Writing Edits (main.tex)

### W1. Rewrite Abstract (lines 53-55) — PRIORITY 1

**Current:** 180 words cramming diagnosis, 54/54 wins, signal ratio, Residual-IA+ 107/123.

**Target (~130 words):**
- Lead with the phenomenon (normalization kills MoE routing)
- Seven causal controls + MI decomposition
- Signal ratio predictor (ρ=-0.88, n=9)
- Fix follows from diagnosis (RR-MoA, 54/54)
- Frozen Paradox (12-79%)
- **Remove** or reduce Residual-IA+ to a single clause ("a dual-stream extension matches DLinear on 5/6 datasets")

### W2. Add "Obvious Fix" Defense (insert after line 340) — PRIORITY 1

New paragraph (~10 lines) after the "Summary of converging controls":
- Acknowledge the fix is simple — argue that's the point
- The contribution is the diagnosis, not the fix
- 11 rescue mechanisms (720 runs) all fail because they address the wrong cause
- Simple fix = correct diagnosis (mirror diagnostic paradigm in medicine/engineering)

### W3. Reframe Contribution (3) (lines 76-77) — PRIORITY 1

**Current:** "Closing the DLinear gap" — invites performance-based evaluation where we lose.

**Target:** "Actionability: the diagnosis predicts that restoring raw-signal access should close the DLinear gap. Residual-IA+ validates this prediction on 107/123 cells." Frame as diagnostic evidence, not performance claim.

### W4. Compress DLinear Gap-Closing in Main Body (lines 370-389) — PRIORITY 2

- Replace Table 5 (`tab:gap_closing_headline`) with a 2-line inline summary
- Move the full table to the appendix
- Saves ~15 lines for the "obvious fix" defense and stronger FT results

### W5. Reframe Proposition 2 (lines 452-469) — PRIORITY 2

- Rename from `\begin{proposition}` to `\begin{observation}` (add `\newtheorem{observation}{Observation}`)
- Add honest framing: "The following decomposition, while algebraically elementary, provides the formal basis for three testable quantitative predictions."
- Keep parts (i)-(iv) and the empirical validation — just don't oversell the algebraic contribution

### W6. Update Frozen Paradox with E1 Results (line 278) — PRIORITY 1 (after E1)

Replace the current 1-sentence extended FT reference with: "Even with careful tuning (lr 1e-3 to 1e-6, 100 epochs, cosine + warmup, layerwise decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation — 90 configurations), the best per-dataset full FT still loses to frozen RR-MoA by [X-Y%]."

### W7. Tighten Conclusion (lines 550-557) — PRIORITY 3

Remove the 107/123 Residual-IA+ sentence. End with: diagnosis → causal controls → RR-MoA fix → Frozen Paradox → practitioner guideline.

### W8. Update verify.py — PRIORITY 2 (after E1)

Add checks for new strong-FT numbers in the extended FT appendix table.

---

## Execution Order

```
Day 1:  Code E1 (run_strong_ft.py) + E2 (hidden_reinjected mode)
        Launch E1 + E2 + E3 on RACE (all can run concurrently with workers)
        Writing: W2 (obvious fix defense), W1 (abstract), W3 (contribution 3)
Day 2:  Writing: W4 (compress DLinear), W5 (Prop 2 reframe), W7 (conclusion)
        Check E1/E2/E3 progress on RACE
Day 3:  Rsync results from RACE
        W6 (update Frozen Paradox with E1 numbers)
        W8 (update verify.py)
        Full build + verify.py pass
Day 4:  Buffer for iterations
```

---

## Verification

1. `python3 evidence_vm/verify.py` — must exit 0 after all edits
2. `pdflatex main.tex` — clean compile, no undefined refs
3. Main body still on page 9 (track line additions/deletions: W2 adds ~10, W4 saves ~15, net -5)
4. All new numeric claims in main.tex have corresponding verify.py checks
5. New experiment JSONs copied to `evidence_vm/` for verification coverage

---

## Expected Impact

| Intervention | Weakness Addressed | Acceptance Δ |
|---|---|---|
| E1 + W6 (strong FT baseline) | #4 Frozen Paradox artifact | +5-8% |
| W2 (obvious fix defense) | #1 Fix is trivial | +3-5% |
| W5 (Prop 2 reframe) | #2 Chain-rule identity | +2-3% |
| W3 + W4 (DLinear de-emphasis) | #3 Gap dilutes story | +3-5% |
| W1 + W7 (focused framing) | #5 Scope creep | +2-3% |

**Estimated post-improvement: 70-80%**

```

162	def _train_adapter_lr(code, model, blocks, X_train, Y_train, X_eval, Y_eval,
163	                      device="cuda", n_epochs=3, forecast_horizon=96, batch_size=128,
164	                      backbone_type="moment", eval_ch=None, scaler=None, lr=1e-4,

172	    exec(code, namespace)
173	    adapter = namespace["Adapter"](hdim, forecast_horizon).to(device)
174	    param_count = sum(p.numel() for p in adapter.parameters())
175	
176	    # Build parameter groups with optional layer-wise LR decay
177	    if layerwise_decay < 1.0 and len(blocks) > 0:
178	        param_groups = [{"params": list(adapter.parameters()), "lr": lr}]
179	        n_blocks = len(blocks)
180	        for i, block in enumerate(blocks):
181	            block_params = [p for p in block.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
182	            if block_params:
183	                depth_from_top = n_blocks - 1 - i
184	                block_lr = lr * (layerwise_decay ** depth_from_top)
185	                param_groups.append({"params": block_params, "lr": block_lr})
186	        optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(param_groups, lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01)
187	    else:
188	        trainable = list(adapter.parameters())
189	        pids = {id(p) for p in trainable}
190	        for p in model.parameters():
191	            if p.requires_grad and id(p) not in pids:
192	                trainable.append(p)
193	                pids.add(id(p))
194	        optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(trainable, lr=lr)
195	
196	    mse_fn = nn.MSELoss()
197	    use_amp = device == "cuda"
198	
199	    loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(
200	        torch.from_numpy(X_train).float(), torch.from_numpy(Y_train).float(),
201	    ), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
202	
203	    # Cosine schedule with warmup
204	    total_steps = n_epochs * len(loader)
205	    warmup_steps = warmup_epochs * len(loader)
206	    scheduler = None
207	    if use_cosine:
208	        from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import CosineAnnealingLR, LinearLR, SequentialLR
209	        schedulers = []
210	        if warmup_steps > 0:
211	            schedulers.append(LinearLR(optimizer, start_factor=0.01, total_iters=warmup_steps))
212	        schedulers.append(CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=total_steps - warmup_steps))
213	        if len(schedulers) > 1:
214	            scheduler = SequentialLR(optimizer, schedulers, milestones=[warmup_steps])
215	        else:
216	            scheduler = schedulers[0]
217	
218	    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
219	        model.train()
220	        adapter.train()
221	        for bx, by in loader:
222	            bx, by = bx.to(device).unsqueeze(1), by.to(device)
223	            mask = torch.ones(bx.shape[0], bx.shape[2], device=device)
224	            with torch.amp.autocast('cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=use_amp):
225	                feat = _extract_features_batch(model, blocks, bx, mask, backbone_type=backbone_type)
226	                loss = mse_fn(adapter(feat), by)
227	            optimizer.zero_grad()
228	            loss.backward()
229	            optimizer.step()
230	            if scheduler is not None:
231	                scheduler.step()
232	
233	    # Evaluate
234	    model.eval()
235	    adapter.eval()
236	    eval_loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(
237	        torch.from_numpy(X_eval).float(), torch.from_numpy(Y_eval).float(),
238	    ), batch_size=batch_size)
239	    preds, tgts = [], []
240	    with torch.no_grad(), torch.amp.autocast('cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=use_amp):
241	        for bx, by in eval_loader:
242	            bx, by = bx.to(device).unsqueeze(1), by.to(device)
243	            mask = torch.ones(bx.shape[0], bx.shape[2], device=device)
244	            preds.append(adapter(_extract_features_batch(
245	                model, blocks, bx, mask, backbone_type=backbone_type)).float().cpu())
246	            tgts.append(by.cpu())
247	
248	    preds, tgts = torch.cat(preds), torch.cat(tgts)
249	    mse = nn.MSELoss()(preds, tgts).item()
250	    mae = nn.L1Loss()(preds, tgts).item()
251	    out = {"mse": mse, "mae": mae, "param_count": param_count}
252	    if eval_ch is not None and scaler is not None:
253	        mse_d, mae_d = compute_denorm_mse(preds, tgts, eval_ch, scaler)
254	        out["mse_denorm"] = mse_d
255	        out["mae_denorm"] = mae_d
256	    return out

324	        """Negative entropy of the router distribution: -H(p).

> AGENT

Interesting — hidden_reinjected collapses to entropy 0.000 and MSE 1.4911 (vs RR-MoA raw 0.680). This is actually a great result for the paper: even re-injecting (μ, σ) into mean-pooled hidden states doesn't recover routing. The hidden states are already homogenized by RevIN before pooling, so adding 2 scalars back to a 512-dim vector is insufficient. This strengthens the "raw input is necessary, not just statistics" argument.

336	In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters---exactly as Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
337	
338	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep eleven standard MoE rescue mechanisms---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, no optimization-side trick can compensate.
339	
340	\textbf{Self-routing and architecture-agnostic validation.} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, we test two additional controls. First, Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA)~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree}: each expert contains its own sigmoid gate---no external router. On raw input, SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). The same architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. Second, replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}). Both confirm the diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. \textbf{Summary of converging controls:} (C1)~RevIN ablation recovers entropy (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, green rows); (C2)~opposite trajectories on MOMENT vs Timer-XL (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}); (C3)~BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm collapse identically (Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}); (C4)~11 rescue mechanisms fail (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}); (C5)~raw-input AdaMix router recovers (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}); (C6)~SR-MoA raw vs hidden ($+87$--$768\%$; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}); (C7)~cross-modality replication on ViT (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}).

74	\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm normalization-specificity.
75	
76	\textbf{(3)~Closing the DLinear gap---and explaining when it cannot close.} Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} adds a raw-input prediction branch and achieves parity-or-better with DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones ($65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses; \S\ref{sec:main_results}). 53	\begin{abstract}
54	Mixture-of-expert adapters with learned routers are a natural way to adapt frozen time series foundation models (TSFMs)---yet they \textbf{catastrophically fail} on TSFMs with instance normalization: routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$ because the normalization strips the per-window statistics the router needs. We isolate this \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse} through seven converging causal controls---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---while all eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism: normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped statistics. The resulting signal-ratio predictor identifies which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$), including where it does \emph{not} help (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA achieves \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$), generalizes across six backbones (two negative controls confirm normalization-specificity), and produces a \textbf{Frozen Paradox} where frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. A dual-stream extension, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}, achieves \textbf{parity-or-better with DLinear on $107/123$ cells} ($65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses), with $15/16$ losses at $H{\geq}192$ and $100\%$ on Timer-XL and Moirai-MoE.
55	\end{abstract}

Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into three components: mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. 553	\section{Conclusion}
554	
555	We identified \emph{normalization-induced co-adaptation} as the root cause of MoE routing collapse on time series foundation models. Seven causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). \textbf{RR-MoA} breaks the collapse by routing on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. A dual-stream extension, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}, matches or beats DLinear on \textbf{108/123 cells} across six backbones---with $15/16$ losses at $H{\geq}192$ and $\mathbf{100\%}$ on Timer-XL and Moirai-MoE.
556	
557	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on \emph{any} normalized backbone (time series, vision, or other modalities), compute the routing signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$. Values above $0.5$ predict that raw routing will help substantially; values below $0.2$ predict it will not (validated cross-modally; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}).
558	
559	\textbf{Limitations.} A small gap remains on ETTh1 ($+2.2\%$ vs DLinear). Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested. Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers only linear backbones, though Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers. $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses only first moments; higher-order statistics may improve prediction on outlier datasets such as Solar.

The $16$ losses cluster at long horizons: $15/16$ at $H{\geq}192$, with the lone $H{=}96$ loss on the smallest dataset (ETTh1, $+2.2\%$). At $H{=}96$, Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} wins $\mathbf{27/27}$ cross-backbone cells (Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}). A dose-response interpolation $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$ reveals a \emph{phase transition} (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs): MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), while entropy stays in $[1.43, 1.57]$---normalization renders routing uninformative without reducing diversity. A temporal-shuffle ablation confirms routing depends on $(M,\Sigma)$ statistics, not temporal ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}

536	\section{Conclusion}
537	
538	We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} as the root cause of MoE adapter failure on time series foundation models. Seven causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{RR-MoA} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. The diagnosis is further validated by its actionability: restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones.
539	
540	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on \emph{any} normalized backbone (time series, vision, or other modalities), compute the routing signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$. Values above $0.5$ predict that raw routing will help substantially; values below $0.2$ predict it will not (validated cross-modally; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}).
541	
542	\textbf{Limitations.} A small gap remains on ETTh1 ($+2.2\%$ vs DLinear). Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested. Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers only linear backbones, though Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers. $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses only first moments; higher-order statistics may improve prediction on outlier datasets such as Solar.
543	
544	\label{page:end_main}
545	\bibliographystyle{plainnat}
```

\newlabel{fig:framework}{{1}{3}{\textbf {RR-MoA architecture.} \textit {Path~A}: the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$ (no gradients through $\theta $). \textit {Path~B}: a lightweight gate reads the raw pre-normalization signal and selects $k$ of $K$ experts via $\mathrm {TopK}$. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf {H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm }0.000$; Table~\ref {tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf {54/54 wins} (Table~\ref {tab:rrmoa})}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:trajectory}{{2}{6}{\textbf {Per-step routing / gradient trajectory} (AdaMix, ETTh1). (a)~Unfrozen+RevIN (red) collapses within ${\sim }50$ steps; frozen (blue) stays stable. Unfrozen \emph {without} RevIN (green dashed) also stays stable. (b)~Dominant expert's gradient grows while others starve (co-adaptation loop, \S \ref {sec:rrmoa})}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:causal_contrast}{{3}{7}{\textbf {Causal contrast: MOMENT vs Timer-XL} (ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing). MOMENT entropy collapses $0.51{\to }0.000$ in ${\sim }40$ steps (red); Timer-XL stays at ${\approx }1.60$ for all $400$ steps (orange). Same code, same data, only normalization differs. Pattern generalizes across all 3 tested datasets}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:dose_response}{{4}{8}{\textbf {Normalization dose-response} (frozen, 5 seeds $\times $ 6 datasets). \textbf {Left:} MSE vs $\alpha $ ($0{=}$raw, $1{=}$RevIN). Phase transition at $\alpha {=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), mild for $\alpha {\leq }0.75$ ($+5.4\%$). \textbf {Right:} entropy stays high at all $\alpha $---normalization renders routing uninformative, not collapsed}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:frozen_paradox}{{5}{9}{\textbf {Left: The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA (blue) beats full fine-tuning (red) by $12$--$79\%$ on all 6 datasets. \textbf {Right: Proposition~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). $R(\mathcal {D})$ predicts where raw routing helps; Traffic and Solar are boundary cases (see text)}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:signal_ratio}{{5}{9}{\textbf {Left: The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA (blue) beats full fine-tuning (red) by $12$--$79\%$ on all 6 datasets. \textbf {Right: Proposition~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). $R(\mathcal {D})$ predicts where raw routing helps; Traffic and Solar are boundary cases (see text)}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_appendix}{{G1}{20}{\textbf {Multi-seed RR-MoA routing weights per dataset} (Top-2 sparse, strictly frozen, mean$\pm $std over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$). Routing is diverse and dataset-dependent: ETTh1 spreads weight roughly uniformly (entropy $1.495\pm 0.034$); ETTm1 concentrates on Last+Max; Weather on Mean+Conv1d}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_viz}{{H2}{21}{\textbf {Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma ) \perp \!\!\!\perp S$ from Proposition~\ref {thm:mi_decomp}(iii)}{figure.2}{}}

On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). 534	Top-2 sparse routing adds only $4.3$\,ms latency ($+10\%$) while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain. Scaling the expert pool from $K{=}3$ to $K{=}20$ changes MSE by less than $5\%$; notably, AdaMix at $K{=}15$ or $20$ maintains high entropy ($2.4$--$2.7$) yet its MSE remains $2$--$6{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA, confirming that the routing failure is informational rather than capacity-limited. RR-MoA's advantage extends beyond the primary horizon: it wins \textbf{24/24} configurations across $H{\in}\{96, 192, 336, 720\}$ and generalizes to imputation ($7/8$ datasets, $-44\%$ to $-77\%$) and classification ($86.5\%$ on BasicMotions; Appendix~\ref{app:topk},~\ref{app:imputation}).}

73:\textbf{(1)~A general principle: normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) proves that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes three \textbf{testable predictions}: (a)~a quantitative predictor $R(\mathcal{D})$ identifies which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) and which do not (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (confirmed: Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~the principle transfers across modalities (confirmed: ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet$+$InstanceNorm2d does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}). Seven converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
337:In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters---exactly as Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
339:\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep eleven standard MoE rescue mechanisms---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, no optimization-side trick can compensate.
532:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone} RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). On Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins \textbf{18/18} by $3$--$31\%$. On Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, which already contains sparse internal experts, RR-MoA still improves \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $37$--$90\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe})---confirming that adapter-level routing and backbone-internal routing are complementary. Two \textbf{negative controls} validate the diagnosis: Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, which lack instance normalization, show no routing collapse (entropy $1.48$--$1.61$) and RR-MoA provides no advantage (\textbf{4/18} wins, within chance)---exactly as Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}).}
967:While the MI decomposition in Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} is algebraically a chain-rule identity, it has deeper information-theoretic content when connected to rate-distortion theory and phase transitions.
970:Instance normalization is a \emph{deterministic lossy compression}: it maps $X \mapsto S$, discarding $(M, \Sigma)$. In rate-distortion theory~\citep{cover2006elements}, this compression has rate $R_\text{strip} = I(X; M, \Sigma \mid S)$ and distortion (for routing) $D_\text{route} = H(E \mid S) - H(E \mid X) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S)$, which is exactly Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i). Under Gaussianity, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ is proportional to the rate-distortion slope at the normalization operating point: it measures how much routing capacity is consumed by the statistics that normalization strips. Specifically, if the joint $(M, \Sigma, S)$ is multivariate Gaussian, then $I(M, \Sigma; E) \propto \log(1 + R(\mathcal{D}))$ (by the Gaussian mutual information formula), making $R(\mathcal{D})$ a \emph{monotone surrogate for the bits lost to normalization}. The validated $\rho = -0.88$ correlation (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}) is thus not a statistical coincidence but a consequence of this rate-distortion structure.
984:The RevIN-encoder pipeline implements a form of the information bottleneck~\citep{tishby2000ib}: it compresses $X$ into a representation $H = f_\theta(S)$ that is optimized for downstream prediction while discarding ``irrelevant'' variability (the per-window location-scale statistics). The routing MI loss from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) is the price paid for this compression \emph{at the routing decision point}. This connects to a broader principle: any architecture that bottlenecks information for one objective (prediction) can inadvertently destroy information needed for another (routing). The vision cross-modality control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) confirms this is not RevIN-specific: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patches creates the same bottleneck, while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does not---because spatial features are not the routing signal for classification.
1290:\textbf{What the router learns.} Per-sample routing decisions correlate with amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$), while Expert~2 (max-pool) handles low-amplitude windows and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude windows. The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the distribution tails, empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$ of Part~(iii) of Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.
1295:\caption{\textbf{Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(iii).}
1301:\textbf{Sufficient statistic router (SSR).} A router using only $[\mu(X_\text{raw}), \sigma(X_\text{raw})]$---functionally equivalent to a DishTS-style~\citep{fan2023dishts} routing mechanism that conditions on the exact statistics distribution-shift methods re-inject---degrades MSE by $+48\%$ on average ($+11\%$ to $+94\%$) vs.\ the Conv1d router across all 8 forecasting datasets. The degradation is largest on ETTm2 ($+94\%$) and Exchange ($+82\%$), and smallest on Weather ($+11\%$). While Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of the information loss, effective routing requires temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale statistics.
1309:\textbf{Statistic-aware information bottleneck (SAIB).} An auxiliary loss forces the router's penultimate representation to predict the window-level $[\mu, \sigma]$---directly operationalizing Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. With SAIB coefficients $\lambda \in \{0.1, 1.0\}$, MSE is unchanged on ETTm1 ($0.395$ vs $0.397$ baseline) and slightly degraded on Weather ($0.250$ vs $0.236$). Routing entropy increases to $1.55$ (near-maximum $\log 5 = 1.61$), indicating the auxiliary loss disperses routing weights without improving forecast accuracy. This confirms the Conv1d router already encodes $\mu, \sigma$ without explicit supervision.
1482:All three normalizers cause entropy collapse to ${\leq}0.004$, while removing normalization entirely keeps entropy stable at $0.817$. The mechanism is the same in each case: the normalizer strips per-window statistics before the encoder, the router receives homogenized hidden states, and gradient co-adaptation amplifies the initial routing bias into full collapse. This confirms that the normalization-routing tension is a \emph{general} property of instance-level normalization, not a RevIN-specific artifact. Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts that collapse occurs specifically when the stripped statistics carry routing signal; a cross-modality control on ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) validates this: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$), while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does \emph{not}---exactly as the theory predicts.
1513:\textbf{Unifying principle.} The collapse mechanism (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}) is modality-general. Whether normalization \emph{triggers} or \emph{prevents} collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal (Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}): ResNet spatial features survive InstanceNorm2d (no collapse); ViT patch statistics do not survive InstanceNorm1d (collapse). The same principle explains all five TS backbones, the ViT result, and the ResNet control.
1618:To test whether gradient descent independently discovers Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}'s prediction, we parameterize the router input as $\mathbf{r} = \sigma(\ell)\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{X}) + (1 - \sigma(\ell))\,\mathbf{X}_{\text{raw}}$, where $\ell$ is a scalar \texttt{nn.Parameter} initialized to $0$ (so $\alpha = \sigma(0) = 0.5$). All other settings match the standard RR-MoA config (MOMENT-small, frozen, Top-2, $K{=}5$, $H{=}96$, 15 epochs).
1639:All 30 runs converge to $\alpha < 0.5$ (range $0.445$--$0.491$), with trajectories monotonically decreasing from the $0.492$ initialization. The unanimity is the key finding: gradient descent independently discovers that raw input carries more routing information, confirming the qualitative prediction of Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. The narrow converged range ($0.459$--$0.482$) means the magnitude does not strongly differentiate datasets---the signal is binary (raw $>$ norm), not graded.
1644:Since the router is deterministic ($E = \arg\max$), $I(X;E) = H(E)$ and the exact MI loss from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) reduces to $H(E \mid S)$. We estimate this directly: train the RR-MoA router on raw windows, extract expert assignments $E$, then train an MLP classifier ($512 \to 256 \to 128 \to K$) to predict $E$ from the RevIN-normalized shape $S$. The held-out cross-entropy (temperature-calibrated) gives $H(E \mid S)$.
1648:\caption{\textbf{Exact MI loss measurement and bound tightness} (3 seeds). $H(E \mid S)$ is the exact routing information lost to normalization. Retention $= I(S;E)/H(E)$. LB = lower bound from Proposition~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii). Gap $= I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ via within-expert CCA.}
